title: Tele-Clearance for Sheriffs' Booking Desks
one_liner: A night-shift nurse-and-NP screening service that lets a rural deputy clear an arrestee for booking from the jail, without spending four hours in the ER while the county goes unpatrolled.
customer: County sheriffs and county commissioners, funded through county risk pools and insurers (for example state association-of-counties liability pools) that pay for jail deaths and lawsuits. Paid per county per month.
problem: Rural jails often have no on-site medical staff, so jail policy requires a hospital 'medical clearance' for any arrestee who is intoxicated, injured or says his chest hurts. At 2am the deputy brings the person to the ER and sits with him for 3-5 hours, sometimes the county's only deputy on duty. The county pays a $2,000-4,000 ER bill and has nobody patrolling. The ER meanwhile holds a bed and a nurse for someone with nothing acutely wrong except being drunk. When clearance is skipped, the risk is a death in custody from alcohol or opioid withdrawal, a head injury or diabetic crisis, which is a lawsuit.
solution: A booking-desk kit (vitals, pulse oximeter, glucometer, breathalyzer, tablet) plus 24/7 on-demand video screening by an RN and NP working from home, using a physician-signed clearance protocol built from ACEP's published best-practice guidance for patients in custody. Dispositions are 'fit for booking with monitoring plan', 'needs ER now', or 're-check in 2 hours'. The service also creates a documented withdrawal-watch checklist, such as sobriety and CIWA-style monitoring, which jails need for liability reasons. The report is time-stamped and defensible.
why_now: Rural hospital and ER closures are lengthening transport times. Prison Policy Initiative reported in October 2025 that about half of incarcerated people are held in rural jails and prisons that risk losing hospital access. Medicaid cuts and the pressure on county budgets are also forcing sheriffs to look for cheaper options, and some already release people on 'medical bond' to avoid ER bills. Telehealth billing and licensure flexibility, together with the Nurse Licensure Compact, make cross-state night staffing workable.
revenue_model: $2,000-3,500 per county per month, including up to about 40 screens. Additional screens are $85 each. Roughly 12 counties would support a team of 6 part-time clinicians. Later, sell an outcome dashboard called 'deputy hours returned to patrol', which is the number commissioners and risk-pool underwriters will care about most.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames the problem as ER wait time or inmate healthcare. From inside the ER, the real cost is the deputy who is stuck with us. In a county with one or two deputies on at night, an ER trip is a public safety hole, and the buyer will pay to close it. Also, most 'medical clearances' are defensive medicine that a good screen would make unnecessary. Big correctional health vendors (Wellpath, NaphCare) sell staffing for large jails and are not built for a 12-bed jail on a county road.
first_30_days: Write the clearance protocol with a supervising physician from a rural ER and get it reviewed by one county attorney. Choose one sheriff the founder already knows from ER encounters. Run a paid pilot at $1,500 for 60 days and count deputy hours saved and ER trips avoided. Then pitch the state's county risk pool and sheriffs' association with the numbers.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: NaphCare (STATCare 24/7 telehealth), Wellpath, Southern Health Partners, Turn Key Health. White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I could run any searches, so this verdict rests on about 14 direct page fetches. That is far short of the 6-12 searches the task called for, and I found no startup-specific evidence either way. I found no vendor whose page shows a tele-clearance product for booking desks, meaning a remote RN/NP screening arrestees before booking with a time-stamped disposition (fit for booking, needs ER now, re-check in 2 hours). Incumbent jail-health vendors (Wellpath, NaphCare, Southern Health Partners) sell on-site staffing or in-custody care. Avel eCare sells 24/7 virtual clinicians to rural ERs and to law enforcement, but only for behavioral crisis. The unserved wedge is a pre-booking, per-county-per-month subscription for jails too small to justify a contracted health vendor, priced against deputy-hours and ER bills. Hospital-run or jail-staff-run tele-clearance programs may already exist locally and I could not check.\n\nTwo structural risks weaken the wedge and need validating early. First, the pitch says the Nurse Licensure Compact makes cross-state night staffing workable, but the NLC covers RNs, not NPs. As far as I know the APRN Compact was not yet operational, so NP staffing likely needs per-state licenses. Second, a remote clinician clearing an intoxicated or injured person on vitals and video alone shifts head-injury and withdrawal liability onto the vendor. That is a malpractice-insurance and clinical-governance problem, and a risk pool may or may not accept it. Revenue is also thin: 12 counties at $2-3.5k a month is roughly $290k-500k a year, with slow county sales cycles.

title: SACCO-Financed Succession Desk, Paid on Milestones
one_liner: A white-label succession desk that payroll SACCOs offer their members: a check-off-repaid 'estate clearing loan' goes into a milestone escrow, and the company earns only as each case step is proven.
customer: The payer and channel is the mid-size payroll or sector SACCO (5k-100k members: teachers, health workers, county staff, police and prison staff) in central and western Kenya, sold to the CEO and credit committee. End users are two groups: salaried members (30-55) whose deceased parent's land is still in a dead name, and heirs of deceased members whose deposits and shares are stuck without a grant. The diaspora child is no longer the only payer.
problem: SACCOs hold two stuck pools. First, deposits and shares of deceased members that cannot be paid out cleanly until heirs produce a grant or agree among themselves (many SACCOs allow small nominee payouts; larger balances and family disputes stall; exact limits to verify): a governance headache, audit query and source of angry families. Second, living members who would borrow large development or mortgage loans against family land, but the land is in a dead person's name so the SACCO cannot take security. Members themselves cannot find a KES 100-250k lump sum for advocate, fees and travel, and distrust strangers who take money for land paperwork, yet they have salaries that can be deducted at source.
solution: The SACCO brands a 'Succession Desk'; the company runs it. Wedge (sellable in 30 days, no SACCO cash outlay): 'Deceased-Member Deposit Clearing'. The SACCO gives a letter of introduction and the list of stuck estates; the company does WhatsApp intake, heir map, consents and field work with a fixed-fee advocate panel; heirs consent in writing to a flat fee deducted from the released deposits. Stage 2, after three or more cases close: 'Estate Clearing Loan' for living members, sized KES 60-250k and repaid by payroll check-off. Proceeds sit in a SACCO-held milestone escrow released at proven steps: heir map and consent pack complete, petition filed and gazetted, confirmation of grant, transmission registered. Advocate fees (from a pre-agreed schedule) and the company's fee are paid from escrow to each party directly against milestones, so the member never hands cash to a stranger and the company never holds client money. At the end the SACCO has a pledgeable title (with heirs' consents to charge) and can pre-approve a development or mortgage loan.
why_now: Payroll SACCOs now run digital member ledgers, USSD and M-Pesa collections, and face competition from banks and digital lenders for their best salaried members, so they want secured, sticky products. Regulator attention on SACCO governance and deceased or dormant member balances (SASRA; verify current rules) makes stuck estates a board-level problem. LLM intake and heir mapping cut the cost of a case enough that a flat KES 12-18k fee works inside a loan. The succession backlog from 1960s-80s allottees is at its peak. Without cheap AI intake the desk would have needed paralegal armies, so this business model did not pencil out in 2019.
revenue_model: Contingent milestone fees of KES 12-18k per estate case, split over the four milestones (for example 40% at consents plus filing, 60% at grant and transmission), funded either from released deposits (deceased-member cases) or from estate clearing loan proceeds via escrow. The company takes no interest and no percentage of estate value. Flat per-loan bounty of KES 3-5k when a cleared title later secures a SACCO loan. After a successful pilot, a white-label desk fee of about KES 150-250k a year per SACCO. Illustration: 10 SACCOs at 100 cases a year each is roughly KES 15M in case fees plus about KES 2M in platform fees (about US$130k), with the SACCOs, not the company, carrying credit risk. The SACCO earns loan interest and clears a liability.
non_obvious_insight: Affordability and trust, not awareness, are the barriers, and the SACCO uniquely owns what neither an advocate nor a startup can: payroll check-off (repayment that costs almost nothing to collect), a welfare touchpoint at the exact moment of a death, and a balance-sheet motive (release stuck deposits, make land pledgeable). The estate clearing loan turns a scary lump sum into a monthly deduction, and the milestone escrow turns a scary stranger into a vendor who is only paid for proven progress. The SACCO's deceased-member float is an embarrassing liability nobody currently sells a fix for.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list 40 SACCOs whose managers you can reach through personal, church, alumni and county networks (teachers', hospital, county-staff SACCOs first). Ask one question: how many deceased-member accounts are pending succession and how many shillings are stuck? Days 10-20: sign two advocates to a fixed-fee panel schedule and draft a one-page pilot contract: SACCO letter of introduction, member-consented flat fee deducted from released deposits, no SACCO cash outlay, so it fits within a CEO's delegated authority and does not need a board vote. Days 20-30: sign one SACCO for 15-20 stuck estates, start intake on the first 5 by WhatsApp, and publish an anonymised 'stuck member deposits' figure to open the next SACCOs. In parallel, draft the estate clearing loan term sheet with that SACCO's credit committee. Metric: days from intake to consents complete, and shillings released per case.
lineage: mutation of I0474 ('Dead Capital: Succession Kits for Diaspora Families'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Luru (open-source 'Kenya's Digital Succession Copilot'), Wakili-Intel (AI drafting copilot for Kenyan advocates), Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority (UFAA), Ardhisasa (Ministry of Lands digital land registry). White space: Provisional, because the web search budget hit its 200-call cap before any search returned results. My evidence comes only from direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches. I found no funded startup, product or open-source project that combines (a) diaspora-paid flat-fee intake, (b) heir mapping across Kenyan name variants, (c) field-agent collection of chief's letters and thumbprint or video consent from 8-20 relatives, and (d) hand-off to partner advocates. The software pieces (family tree, readiness score, drafting copilots) exist only as zero-star hobby repos. Government platforms (Ardhisasa, court e-filing, UFAA) cover filing and claiming but not multi-heir coordination. UFAA's beneficiary claim rule makes succession a prerequisite for claiming a dead person's unclaimed assets, so a succession-first product that unlocks those assets has a logical hook. The unserved wedge is the coordination and evidence-gathering layer sold to the paying sibling abroad. It is still unproven whether ordinary advocates or land-buying-company agents already do this informally, because I could not search for them. | How this version avoids them: Fixed-fee advocates (the direct competitor) sit on the panel and are paid directly from escrow, so the desk is their referral source rather than their rival, and no fee is split with a non-lawyer. Luru and Wakili-Intel have no distribution, field agents or financing and are zero-star hobby projects. UFAA is unaffected because the desk clears the SACCO's own liabilities, not UFAA assets. Ardhisasa and e-filing are systems the panel files into. Competing on a different axis (who pays and how): individual advocates cannot offer financing or escrow; banks will not run rural field operations; SACCOs will not build LLM intake and consent ops in-house. Switching costs come from integration with the SACCO's loan system, panel and escrow, and it does not depend on the parent's unproven diaspora willingness to pay.

title: Appraisal Workfile Trustee for Retired and Deceased Appraisers
one_liner: A neutral custodian that holds a retiring or deceased appraiser's workfiles for 10 years, proves they were never altered, and answers subpoenas, board letters and lender QC requests so the retiree or widow never has to.
customer: Wedge: sole-proprietor certified residential appraisers aged 62+ who have just gone inactive or announced retirement in 3-4 states (TX, OH, PA, CO), plus heirs and executors of appraisers who die or become incapacitated. These people usually already hold a free LIA or OREP retirement tail, so the money risk is covered and the missing piece is the defense file. Scale payers: E&O administrators and state appraiser associations (loss-control benefit). Requesters (attorneys, lenders, boards) pay production fees where rules allow.
problem: USPAP requires workfiles to be retained and retrievable for at least 5 years (or 2 years after a judicial proceeding ends), and regulators can act later. A retiree's copy sits on an aging laptop, a USB drive or a software subscription that lapses. The free tail pays defense costs but does not preserve or produce the file, and a workfile with no independent proof of when it was finalized is easy to attack as backfilled. When an appraiser dies, board letters and subpoenas land on a widow with no idea what a workfile is. Nobody answers a subpoena on the retiree's behalf: software vendors store files, they do not act as agent.
solution: Product v1, 'Seal and Hold': (1) A 60-minute import from a la mode, ClickFORMS or ACI exports or a drive image. Every file is hashed and stamped with a third-party RFC 3161 timestamp, kept in write-once encrypted storage with an index by date, client and address. (2) A custodian agreement naming the Trustee as records custodian and agent for production, plus a notice letter to the state board. (3) A production desk that handles subpoenas, board requests, lender QC and repurchase requests and E&O carrier requests, notifies the retiree or estate, and bills the requester. (4) An estate trigger: named heirs, a death or incapacity switch and pre-filled paperwork. (5) Retention beyond the minimum, with legal-hold extension. Deliberately excluded: trainees, client transfer, earn-outs, tail brokerage.
why_now: UAD 3.6 becomes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 and is pushing veterans to quit rather than relearn. WorkingRE's 2026 survey says 31% plan to leave within 3 years and 57% are over 60, so a predictable wave of exits is starting. Free LIA and OREP tails have made the money side a solved problem, which leaves the file as the remaining exposure. Immutable cold storage and third-party timestamping are commodity-cheap, so intake per retiree is under an hour of ops time.
revenue_model: $695 one-time for 10-year custody including 3 productions (or $19/month). $995 estate or heir rush plan. Extra productions at $195-450, requester-pays where state rules permit, otherwise billed to the retiree or estate. Group license to E&O administrators and associations at roughly $8-15 per insured per year as loss control (needs validation). Cold storage for about 100 GB costs around $1 per month, so gross margin is 85%+ and the real cost is the production desk and counsel. A two-person team breaks even around 500 custodies a year (assumption).
non_obvious_insight: The free tail pays the lawyer, but a claim is won or lost on whether the appraiser can produce a file that provably existed in that form on that date. A retiree's own drive cannot prove non-alteration, while a neutral custodian with hash chains and third-party timestamps can. So this is closer to a notary or escrow than to storage, which is why software vendors paid by the user cannot credibly sell it and why insurers, estates and boards have reasons to care. Once the custodian is named in the retiree's board and carrier paperwork, moving away means new attestations, which creates switching costs.
first_30_days: Week 1: retain counsel for the custodian agreement and a state-by-state memo on retention, board notification, subpoena handling, and confirmation that we are not acting as an appraiser or AMC and no fee-splitting rule applies. Pull public rosters for TX, OH, PA and CO and flag licenses that went inactive or expired in the last 24 months and active licensees licensed 25+ years. Week 2: call 20 of them and pre-sell at $695 with a refund guarantee, then concierge-deliver the first 5 by hand (import 5 years of workfiles, timestamp, issue a custody certificate). Kill rule: fewer than 6 of 20 pay means pivot to insurer-funded only. Week 3: ask LIA and OREP claims managers, two independent E&O agents and one state appraiser association how workfile requests reach them today and whether they would co-brand or fund it as loss control. Meet 3 estate-planning attorneys. Week 4: run a 'What happens to your files when you retire' session through Appraisal Institute chapters and appraiser forums and target 15 paid custodies.
lineage: mutation of I1039 ('Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: LIA Administrators (Appraisal Institute-endorsed E&O program), OREP (Appraisal Insurance), a la mode TOTAL / Cotality (also ACI, ClickFORMS), Aloft Appraisal. White space: No company found that bundles the four pieces (workfile custody plus subpoena and board-inquiry response, tail, local-knowledge capture, direct-lender client handoff to a supervised successor). Searches for retiring-appraiser succession services, workfile custodian services, and appraiser practice brokers returned only DIY articles from WorkingRE, McKissock, Appraisal Today and NAR.

Specific white space that survives:
(1) Third-party workfile custody and retrieval (agent-of-record for subpoenas and board requests) for retired or deceased appraisers. USPAP requires retention and retrievability for 5+ years, with regulators able to act later, and no dedicated vendor was found. Software vendors and cloud storage only store files, and nobody answers a subpoena for you.
(2) Local, rural or community-lender-funded succession. Aloft, Valligent and Solidifi are national or AMC-centric, not local continuity for a single county.
(3) The retiree-as-mentor stipend and earn-out structure, which none of the trainee programs use.

Specific weaknesses in the idea:
(a) The 'tail is frightening and costly' pain is largely solved for long-tenured appraisers by free LIA and OREP retirement tails. The paid pain is limited to those with short E&O tenure, gaps, or sub-5-year policies. Tail brokerage commissions are therefore thin.
(b) Fee-splitting and finder's-fee rules. Minnesota (82B.20) bans commission-splitting, rebates and finder's fees with appraisers, and other states have similar rules. An earn-out on inherited client revenue and a 20-30% take on trainee fees may be illegal in some states unless structured as a sale of a business or as employment.
(c) Supervisor-of-record is not passive. State rules limit trainee counts (Aloft cites 3 per supervisor), require certification in good standing and the supervisor's own E&O, and make the supervisor take full responsibility. A retiree who stays on as supervisor is not really retired and keeps license, CE and E&O costs.
(d) Client transferability is weak. Appraisal Today notes practices under $200K are 'buying a job', and residential lender relationships are 'fickle'. Most practices sell at 0.33-0.5x revenue with seller financing, and AMC-dependent revenue is not transferable.
(e) Pipeline substitutes are growing: PAREA, AXIS/CRN trainee-inspection reform, Valligent and Aloft paying supervisors. | How this version avoids them: LIA and OREP sell tail money, not file preservation or production, so they are complements and a possible channel rather than rivals. a la mode/Cotality, ACI and ClickFORMS store files for a paying user but do not act as agent of record, sign attestations or answer subpoenas, and a vendor would take on legal exposure for a lapsed customer, so it is unlikely to respond soon. Aloft, Valligent, Solidifi, AXIS and PAREA are all trainee and supervisor plays, and this idea leaves that lane completely, which also removes the supervisor-of-record burden and trainee-count limits. AppraiseItNow buys only non-residential and specialty practices and offers no custody. Reggora and the AMC consolidators (Class Valuation, Atlas VMS) target lenders and AMC capacity, not individual retirees. Dropping earn-outs, percentage-of-trainee-fees and client transfer removes the fee-splitting, minimum-legal and weak-transferability flaws the research flagged.

title: Deficiency-Suit Add-On Credit Audits for Consumer Defense Firms
one_liner: A flat-fee, 24-hour audit that rebuilds a repossession deficiency from the retail installment contract and shows the unearned add-on credits, notice defects and fee errors the lender or debt buyer left out, sold to the consumer-defense lawyers who already have the client and the deadline.
customer: Consumer-defense and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid offices that defend post-repossession deficiency suits. Start in two or three states chosen from docket data in week 1 (candidates: Maryland, Pennsylvania, Ohio, where notice rules and fee-shifting tend to favor borrowers; confirm before committing). Wedge buyer: small consumer-law firms of 1 to 10 lawyers that take flat-fee or fee-shifting cases, plus 3 to 5 legal aid units.
problem: A repossessed borrower is typically sued 6 to 18 months later, often by a debt buyer, on a one-line balance backed by a thin affidavit. The defense lawyer has about 30 days to answer, no numbers person, and a flat fee or grant-funded hours. The deficiency figure usually does not credit the unearned GAP, service-contract and other add-ons that were rolled into the loan, and may carry defective post-sale notices or inflated fees. Rebuilding it by hand takes a paralegal hours, so most defendants default or settle blind. The parent's borrower-side value is real but lacked a buyer with standing, a deadline and a fee-shifting statute. This buyer has all three.
solution: The attorney uploads the complaint, contract image, pre- and post-sale notices and auction bill. Within 24 hours the tool returns a Deficiency Autopsy PDF: (1) a rebuilt ledger from the retail installment contract (amount financed, itemized add-ons, finance charge, payments, fees); (2) unearned add-on credits owed under the contract and state rule, with the administrator's cancellation requirement and a computed pro-rata figure; (3) a notice checklist against UCC Article 9 and the state motor-vehicle finance act (timing, required content, explanation of the deficiency calculation, commercial-reasonableness red flags such as sale price versus wholesale value, and whether a defective notice bars the deficiency in that state); (4) an exposure sheet covering offsets, defenses and potential statutory damages under UCC 9-625(c)(2) as adopted by the state; (5) draft answer paragraphs, counterclaim language and targeted discovery requests aimed at cancellation records. A human analyst reviews every output at first, later only exceptions. Flat fee only, never a share of a fee award, which avoids fee-sharing problems with non-lawyers (Rule 5.4) and keeps this an attorney work tool rather than advice to consumers.
why_now: Subprime 60+ day delinquency hit a 32-year high in January 2026 and roughly 3M repossessions a year feed a deficiency pipeline that debt buyers monetize through suits. 84-month loans and underwater trade-ins make deficiencies large, so a $99 audit is small next to the dollars at stake per case. LLMs now read messy contract scans, auction bills and notices for cents per case, which was not economic in 2022. Federal consumer-finance enforcement has retrenched since 2025 (verify), so what enforcement remains is private and state-level, and it runs through exactly these lawyers.
revenue_model: $99 per audit; $499 per month for up to 8 audits plus template library for small firms; about $2,400 per year site licenses for legal aid; $750 for attorney-directed analyst declarations. Second, higher-value stream: anonymized pattern reports on defect prevalence by lender, debt buyer and collection law firm (for example, the share of one plaintiff's notices that omit add-on credits), sold to class-action firms and state AG staff at $25K to $100K per report. Audit revenue alone is a small wedge (likely single-digit millions a year), so the dataset and pattern reports are the scale path.
non_obvious_insight: Each audit is a product and a labeled data point. Deficiency defects are systematic because one plaintiff's template produces the same omission in every case, and UCC 9-625 statutory damages attach per consumer, so the pattern is worth far more to class counsel than a single case is to a defendant. The parent's flaw, that lender incentives run against the borrower, becomes the moat: lenders and their in-house recovery teams can never sell this because they are the party being audited. The borrower's claim also needs a number and a deadline, not the dealer's or administrator's cooperation.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull about 300 recent deficiency complaints from public dockets in the candidate states (plaintiff, amount, whether the defendant had counsel) to pick two states and list the 10 heaviest filers; have a consumer-law ethics lawyer review the template for unauthorized-practice and fee-sharing risk. Weeks 2 to 3: ask 15 consumer-defense firms and 3 legal aid units (through NACA, NCLC and state consumer-law listservs) for their next 3 deficiency cases free in return for a written outcome; deliver each audit manually in 24 hours using LLM extraction plus an analyst. Week 4: switch to $99, publish an anonymized 'five places deficiency numbers lie' guide, and log the dollar swing on every case. Target: 30 audits delivered, 10 paid, 5 documented cases where the balance moved by more than $1,000.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Origence (formerly CU Direct) - loan origination/indirect platform (CUDL), Assurant (F&I administrator and TPA), Unverified: consumer GAP/VSC refund-claim services (contingency), Unverified: in-house lender recovery and collections teams and BPO vendors. The WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before I could run any queries, and only about 15 direct URL fetches were possible, many of which 404'd or were blocked. That leaves three points.

1. I found no direct competitor selling a payoff-triggered GAP/VSC refund plug-in to credit unions. Origence, the dominant CU indirect-lending platform, and Assurant, a major administrator, show no such product on their homepages.

2. Genuinely unserved and specific, if the market read holds:
   - A per-payoff, lender-integrated refund workflow for dealer-sold, financed add-ons at credit unions.
   - A 50-state pro-rata rules engine combined with an administrator-by-administrator cancellation-requirements database.
   - An attorney-ready audit of repossession deficiency notices that reconciles unearned add-on credits. Consumer-bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid are plausible buyers, because the lender's or dealer's incentive runs against the borrower.

3. Weaknesses in the idea as written, from reasoning rather than found evidence:
   - The claim that the lender never owned the product is shaky. Under many state retail installment sales acts, and under the FTC Holder Rule, the assignee or holder can carry refund and credit obligations. That helps demand, as a compliance and UDAAP driver, but it changes the pitch from 'find hidden money' to 'reduce liability'.
   - A 20-30% success fee taken from a member's own refund has poor fee optics for a credit union. It also conflicts with the idea's own member-experience rationale.
   - On payoff, the refund goes to the borrower, so the CU gets no direct economic benefit. The CU's incentive is goodwill and compliance, not revenue.
   - CU vendor due diligence and core/LOS integration will make the sales cycle slow.
   - The California SB 766 citation in the idea did not check out. The leginfo summary I fetched for the 2023-24 bill described an unrelated social-worker licensing bill. Do not rely on that cite until it is confirmed. | How this version avoids them: Consumer refund sites and SEO players wait for a borrower to find them and cannot touch deficiency suits; here the lawyer is already retained. Origence and other LOS vendors are irrelevant: no lender integration, no credit-union sales cycle, and they would never build a product that audits their own customers. Assurant and other administrators become a data source, not a target. In-house lender recovery teams and BPOs, the direct overlap flagged in the parent research, become the counterparty whose numbers are being audited. General legal-tech (Clio, Filevine, CoCounsel-style research tools) is horizontal and has no contract-to-notice reconciliation or administrator rules. The real substitute is hourly forensic accountants and paralegals at several hundred dollars a case, which a $99 audit undercuts. Competitor research was not fully verified: check for existing auto-deficiency audit vendors before building.

title: Credit Bureau for Federal Drug-Refund Receivables
one_liner: Invert lend-and-learn into learn-and-license. A consortium data utility and certified servicer that makes Medicare price-negotiation refunds, later 340B rebates and Part B refunds, a standard scorable collateral class for any lender, wholesaler or credit fund.
customer: First wave is 8-15 specialty lenders, regional banks with pharmacy desks, and family offices or credit funds that already lend to pharmacies or want to. Corporate Capital Direct, ARF, Fora and similar firms, and regional banks, are the named types. Later customers are wholesalers, insurers and note buyers. Pharmacies and hospitals are data suppliers, not customers. They consent because their lender then advances more, faster and cheaper.
problem: Every lender that could fund the refund float meets the same gaps. They cannot verify which claims are MFP-eligible, aged or disputed. They have no dilution history, no controlled payment route and no standard documents. Collateral is invisible to them, so they treat it as ineligible or advance blind at 50-75%. Each lender sees only its own few borrowers, too small a sample to price dilution, so capital does not flow to a float of $500M+ a month. The same gap will repeat in 340B rebate floats (Health Affairs estimates $8.9M-$208M a year per hospital) and in Part B refunds when the 2028 drug cohort arrives.
solution: Product ladder. 1) Within 6 months, the MFP Borrowing-Base Certificate, a portal and API. A lender invites a borrower, the borrower connects a read-only PMS export and the MTF remittance files, and we return a weekly certificate listing eligible refund receivables by claim, age, dilution score, dispute status, recommended reserve and exceptions, with alerts when refunds miss 14- and 21-day marks. 2) The consortium. Anonymized claim-to-refund outcomes from all lenders' borrowers feed a Refund Dilution Index by manufacturer, drug and pharmacy type (median days to pay, reversal and rejection rates), published quarterly. Contributing outcomes is a condition of use, as with credit-bureau furnishing. 3) Standard paper. A master receivables purchase agreement, control-agreement templates and a certified-servicer mark. 4) Later, servicer-of-record and small risk retention on pooled notes sold to insurers and credit funds, and extension to 340B rebate refunds and Part B refunds. Claim data can contain PHI, so we use minimum-necessary fields and business associate agreements from day one.
why_now: The refund class is nine months old and has no standard, no data owner and no legal template. Two expansions are scheduled (semaglutide and 14 more drugs in January 2027, another cohort in 2028). Private credit is hungry for short-duration paper whose obligors are large manufacturers. CMS and HRSA policy keeps shifting, which favors a utility that spans programs over a single-program lender. The MTF remittance and 835 files are standardized, so ingestion is buildable by a small team in months.
revenue_model: Subscription of about $150-$300 a month per monitored borrower, plus about 15-25 bps annualized on certified balances. Index licensing to funds at about $25-100k a year. Later, 30-50 bps servicing on pooled receivables and a 5% retained slice of notes. Illustrative first year: 10 lenders, 600 monitored borrowers and $36M certified is roughly $1.1-1.9M of recurring revenue. The upside is in scale, since each additional program (340B, Part B) reuses the same engine and consortium.
non_obvious_insight: Credit bureaus and ABL field examiners exist because collateral quality is unobservable to lenders. Here it is observable, but only in files that sit in the pharmacy. Whoever collects the first 20 lenders' claim-to-refund outcomes owns the only labeled dataset of statutory-refund dilution, and it compounds, since each new lender lowers every other lender's losses. It also hedges policy risk. If CMS speeds refunds, the index shows it and lenders shift to cheaper advance rates. If not, the float grows and demand rises. The standard travels to other federal refund flows. A single-program lender cannot make that claim.
first_30_days: Build ingestion for the three most common pharmacy management system exports and the MTF remittance files, using files from about 10 pharmacies. Approach 15 lenders and family offices with a free 60-day shadow certificate on three of their existing pharmacy borrowers, in exchange for outcome data and a design-partner letter of intent. Sign 2-3 letters of intent. Put together the borrower consent template and business associate agreement with a healthcare privacy attorney. Sound out one credit fund on eventually buying certified pools.
lineage: mutation of I0499 ('Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SpendMend (MFP Rebate Reconciliation), Plenful (MFP Intelligence / MFP Command Center), ScriptPro Financial Advantage, Liberty Software (and other PMS vendors, e.g. PioneerRx, PrimeRx, Redsail). White space: Verdict: gap, and a narrow one. In roughly 27 searches across varied terms (MFP refund advance, bridge loan, factoring, fintech, PSAO program, wholesaler program) I found NO product that specifically underwrites and advances against MTF-remitted MFP refunds. Pharmacy lenders sell generic A/R and MCA lines, and the MFP players only sell reconciliation. The unserved space is a claim-level underwriting and servicing capability for refund dilution risk: 340B lesser-of rejections (RARC N907 inappropriate rejections), reversals, Good Faith Inquiry disputes, and authorized-generic refund amounts. It is most valuable for borrowers whose float is large: LTC/senior-care pharmacies, 5-50 store groups, and possibly 340B covered entities in the HRSA rebate pilot, where the float is $8.9M-$208M a year for hospitals (Health Affairs). It also applies to the January 2027 step-up when semaglutide joins.

The wedge is weak in five ways.
1. The 'free missing-refund report' is already crowded: SpendMend, Plenful ($76M raised), ScriptPro, Liberty, and free Beacon MFP dashboards.
2. A typical independent's float is small, about $11k a week or $27k a month per NCPA. At 15-25% APR that is roughly $4-7k a year of gross revenue per pharmacy, before losses and a cost of funds of 8-10%. Customer acquisition through state associations and Facebook groups will be costly relative to that.
3. Wholesalers control the payment path. Cardinal routes MFP refunds through Central Pay and wholesalers auto-debit weekly, so a lender's sweep sits behind the wholesaler in practice. Cardinal customers cannot easily direct refunds to a lender-controlled account.
4. 'Non-recourse' is hard to deliver. Manufacturers can reverse refunds and CMS's own materials describe reversals when claims prove ineligible, so a lender will need pharmacy recourse or holdbacks. That undermines the 'prime paper' insight.
5. Policy is a moving target. CMS made manufacturers include cash-flow mitigation plans in their MFP effectuation plans (accelerated refunds, self-identification). NCPA is still pushing CMS and manufacturers for faster payment, including in Sept 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance.

Adjacent generic lenders can also just add MFP refunds to a borrowing base.

Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and open-source sweeps were not fully run. 'No direct competitor found' means not found, not proven absent. | How this version avoids them: SpendMend, Plenful and ScriptPro sell workflow to the pharmacy or health system, and their data is siloed per customer. They are not lender-grade certificates and not a consortium. Beacon and CMS give free dashboards to dispensing entities, not to lenders. Corporate Capital Direct, Live Oak, ARF, Fora and wholesalers become customers instead of competitors, and we never fight for the pharmacy relationship. We can even ingest SpendMend and Plenful outputs as data sources. The main threat is Plenful adding a lender module. The defenses are lender-neutral consortium data that a single vendor cannot replicate, and a certified-servicer standard that lenders can rely on and a wholesaler such as Cardinal cannot credibly be neutral about.

title: Dairy-Backed Calf Guarantee Pool With Immune Screening
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of selling buyers a verification and later insuring the raiser, make the dairy, who controls colostrum, warrant its own graded calves for 21 days, with our grade as the price of admission and a reserve pool we administer, growing into a mutual or captive with an MGA and reinsurer behind it.
customer: Large dairies (roughly 1,000+ cows, which now sell hundreds to a couple thousand crossbred calves a year, a $0.5-2M line that they still treat as a sideline) that already run good colostrum programs (pasteurized colostrum, Brix testing) and are irritated at being priced at the herd average. First: 3-5 dairies in one region. Second payer: the raisers who pay a premium for guaranteed calves. Later: an insurer or MGA taking over the pool's tail risk.
problem: A dairy with excellent colostrum management cannot credibly say so, so it gets the average price. Buyers cannot underwrite the calves, and insurers cannot underwrite a raiser's loss because the raiser's housing and feeding confound the cause of death (the parent's own moral hazard problem), and federal Livestock Risk Protection excludes mortality and disease. Both sides distrust each other's numbers, and the grade alone still leaves the raiser holding the risk. The dairy owns the biggest early-death driver and holds none of the downside.
solution: Each enrolled dairy has every calf graded at day 3-5 by us. Excellent and Good calves get a Guaranteed tag: if a calf dies of covered causes (neonatal scours, sepsis, weak-calf, navel) within 21 days of delivery, the buyer gets a replacement or price credit up to the lot price. Claims are adjudicated by us using tag custody, necropsy photos or vet note and treatment log within 72 hours. Trauma and raiser-negligence exclusions plus a small buyer co-pay keep the raiser's incentives in play. The dairy pays a per-calf assessment into a segregated reserve we administer, priced by grade and falling as the dairy's grade mix improves, so fixing colostrum is directly rewarded. Poor calves are sold openly at a discount without a guarantee. Unused reserve is rebated at year end, mutual style. Stage 2 (about 50,000 graded calves): a licensed MGA with a fronting carrier and stop-loss reinsurance. Stage 3: a risk retention group or captive owned by participating dairies.
why_now: Beef-on-dairy volume is heading from about 3.2M toward the 5-6M CattleFax projects, at four-figure prices, so a dairy's calf revenue is finally large enough to fund a guarantee and its reputation is worth protecting. A published four-tier standard gives a shared, auditable eligibility rule. Packers already penalize unknown health history and the heifer shortage makes each lost calf expensive to replace, so buyers want risk transfer more than they want a certificate. Cheap custody capture makes claims adjudicable at a few dollars per claim.
revenue_model: $5 per graded calf plus 15-25% administration and commission on guarantee assessments (assessments of about $15-30 per guaranteed calf, in line with an expected covered-loss cost near $15-20 on a $1,200 calf at 1.5% early loss, to be checked against real data), plus profit commission from the reinsurer and float on reserves. Dairy economics: a $35-60 buyer premium against a $15-30 assessment, so about $15-25 net per calf. On 1,000 calves that is a modest but real $15-25K a year. Mature sizing: 500K guaranteed calves a year is about $5M in fees and commissions, with a $10-30M revenue ceiling at 1-2M calves, if the pool becomes the industry standard. The moat is the dataset, the escrow role and the mutual's membership, not the refractometer.
non_obvious_insight: A guarantee is the cheapest credible signal there is (Spence): a seller who will pay if the calf dies proves quality without the buyer trusting any measurement. It also flips the moral hazard. In the first 21 days the risk is controlled by the party paying for it, the dairy, which is why insuring the raiser is hard and warranting the dairy's calves is not. The grade becomes the actuarial rate table rather than a label, and dairies with bad colostrum programs are priced out until they fix them, which turns a data business into a compliance flywheel.
first_30_days: Days 1-14: sign 3-5 large dairies with pasteurized colostrum programs, plus one raiser or broker who will state a premium for guaranteed calves. Draft a one-page 21-day replacement-credit warranty (covered causes, exclusions, 72-hour claim rule, cap at lot price) and get it reviewed by an ag attorney, since a seller's own warranty is a sale-of-goods term but pooling across sellers may be insurance under state law. Open an escrow account. Days 15-30: grade and guarantee a 1,000-calf pilot with each dairy prefunding a $20 per calf reserve. Run the 21-day window and publish the claims ratio. Gates: claims under 80% of assessments and the buyer pays $35 or more a head over the ungraded price. If claims are high, reprice or drop the dairy. Stage 2 only after 50,000 graded calves and a signed MGA term sheet.
lineage: mutation of I0617 ('Immune-Graded Beef-on-Dairy Calves With Warranty'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Where Food Comes From (third-party verification: Age Verification, Source Verification, USDA Process Verified Program, custom Process Verified claims), Calftech Corporation (Central Valley, CA calf ranch). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I could not run the planned searches on Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or vendor names. The 'nobody does this' finding therefore rests on direct page fetches and a GitHub repository search, not full web coverage. My early attempts to pull search-engine result pages through WebFetch returned junk or CAPTCHAs, and I stopped them because they sidestep the search limit. The verdict is low-to-moderate confidence.

What I found:
- No company selling per-calf independent Brix or serum total protein grading with a QR passport, and no calf-immunity warranty product. Where Food Comes From has no such program. Vytelle's site lists no calf program. GitHub has no relevant open-source tool, only hobby repos.
- Livestock Risk Protection explicitly 'does not protect against mortality, condemnation, physical damage or disease' (https://agproud.com/articles/60060-knowledge-is-the-best-insurance-an-overview-of-livestock-risk-protection). Federal cover for calf death loss is therefore absent. I did not verify what private mortality insurance exists.

What still stands in the way, and is not competition in the strict sense:
1. Self-testing. A raiser can Brix-test at arrival for about $1, and dairies can test their own calves. Independent custody only earns money where seller and buyer distrust each other's numbers, or where price is set before arrival.
2. Bilateral history. Feeders already ask which dairy the calves came from and some supply sire straws to dairies (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). Source-dairy reputation substitutes for per-calf grading.
3. Warranty moral hazard. Immunity is one driver of loss, but raiser housing, feeding and biosecurity dominate, which makes underwriting hard. Lombard's consensus paper puts failure of passive transfer at roughly twice the risk, which is a useful signal but not a full loss model.
4. Incumbents can absorb it. Verifiers, diagnostics vendors, calf-ranch networks and packer programs could add an immunity field.

Genuinely unserved: an independent, per-calf immunity record that travels from dairy to raiser to feeder to packer, plus a neutral dispute-resolution measurement. | How this version avoids them: Where Food Comes From is a verifier and does not take underwriting positions or hold per-calf outcome data, so it can be a claims-audit partner rather than a rival. Calftech-style integrated ranches earn credibility by owning both ends and keeping data in-house. This gives any dairy the same credibility without owning a ranch, as a capital-light replica of vertical integration, and integrated operators simply become additional buyers of guaranteed calves. The parent's stated obstacles are answered directly. Self-testing is irrelevant because the guarantee, not the number, carries the trust. Bilateral history is replaced by a financial commitment. Warranty moral hazard is contained by a short window on dairy-controlled causes, exclusions and a co-pay. No federal mortality cover exists (LRP excludes it), and I could not verify what private livestock mortality insurance exists, so the plan partners with an MGA instead of competing with one.

title: Contingency Recovery of Unpaid Implant Carve-Outs
one_liner: Find and collect the implant and device carve-out payments that hospitals and surgery centers are owed but never bill, because the invoice lives in accounts payable and not in the billing office.
customer: Physician-owned spine and orthopedic ASCs, plus small and mid-size hospital ortho/spine/cardiac service lines, with commercial payer contracts that carve out implants. Paid 20-30% of recovered dollars.
problem: Many commercial contracts pay implants and high-cost devices separately, at invoice cost plus a markup, but only if the vendor invoice is submitted with the claim. The implant log is in the OR record, the invoice is in supply chain or AP, and the claim is built by billing. Nobody connects them. The claim goes out with L8699 or revenue code 027x lines at billed charges, and the payer pays $0 for the device or folds it into the case rate. The payment posts as 'paid', so nobody notices the loss. This is $5k-$50k per case for spine and joint work.
solution: Ingest the implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers), AP invoice PDFs (parsed with an LLM), contract carve-out terms extracted from the PDFs, and the 837/835 files. Compute expected carve-out payment versus actual, auto-assemble invoice attachments per payer rules, and file corrected claims and appeals inside timely-filing windows. Run it as a service for the first clients (manual, coder-led), then automate the matching.
why_now: CMS's CY2026 outpatient rule began phasing out the inpatient-only list and added many procedures, mostly musculoskeletal, to the ASC-covered list. More device-heavy spine and ortho cases are moving to ASCs whose small billing staffs have never dealt with carve-outs. Payers are also using AI-driven payment integrity that makes missing attachments an automatic zero.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered carve-out payments. After the first recovery, convert to $1.5-4k/month prospective monitoring per facility.
non_obvious_insight: The loss is invisible in every standard revenue-cycle KPI. Denial rate looks fine and AR looks fine because the line paid 'as billed under the case rate'. The only way to see it is to lay the supply chain invoice next to the contract term next to the 835. Billers know it happens. Supply chain does not know payers pay for it. Finance never audits it. That gap between three departments is the earned secret.
first_30_days: Pick 10 physician-owned spine and ortho ASCs through ASCA chapters and surgeon-owner LinkedIn outreach. Offer a free 90-day lookback audit, since contingency means zero risk to them. Each needs to share 835s, implant logs, invoices and the top three commercial contracts. Do the first three audits by hand with a coder and a spreadsheet, and use the dollars found as the sales collateral. Then automate the invoice parsing.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Aspirion (ContractIQ, payment variance recovery), FinThrive (Contract Manager, A/R Optimizer, Revenue Integrity), Sift Healthcare (RevProtect), Waystar (Claim Attachments, Denial Recovery, Recoupment Manager). White space: Caveat on confidence: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before any of my searches ran, so the competitor check is thinner than requested. It rests on direct fetches of about 15 vendor and trade-publication pages plus Becker's ASC on-site search result pages. The Becker's article bodies returned 403. Crunchbase, Reddit and Product Hunt were not reachable. I found no dedicated competitor doing what this idea describes, and I could not check the many small RCM and consulting shops that a live web search would surface. I also could not confirm Cloudmed/R1 or Experian Contract Manager features (the R1 URL 404'd). Both are plausible incumbents with contract modeling.

What looks unserved, and is specific: (1) a contingency service focused only on the implant/device carve-out. It would join the OR implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers) to the AP vendor invoice, then to the payer contract carve-out clause, then to the 835 line. None of the general underpayment vendors above advertise this. (2) The buyer is the physician-owned spine/ortho ASC. Enterprise tools like Sift, FinThrive and Aspirion are aimed at health systems. (3) The claim-side fix is assembling the invoice attachment per payer rules and filing a corrected claim inside timely-filing limits. General contract-modeling tools mostly stop at flagging a variance.

Risks to the premise:
- 'Nobody connects them' is overstated. Becker's ran 'ASC Implant Carve-Outs: Opportunities, Challenges & 4 Best Practices' in 2014, so ASC operators know carve-outs exist (https://www.beckersasc.com/asc-coding-billing-and-collections/asc-implant-carve-outs-opportunities-challenges-4-best-practices/). ASC-specialist billers such as SIS/Surgical Notes, National Medical Billing Services and Nimble probably submit implant invoices as routine, so the addressable leakage may sit mostly in ASCs with weak or outsourced generalist billing.
- Any player with a contingency model and payer-contract modeling could add this quickly. Aspirion's ContractIQ is the most obvious.
- Medicare does not carve out implants in the ASC setting, so this is a commercial-contract play only. Each payer contract must be read individually, which limits how far it scales.
- I could not verify the CY2026 IPO-list phase-out and ASC list additions cited in the idea's why-now. CMS's page confirms only that a CY2026 ASC final rule (CMS-1834-FC) exists.

title: Private Road Associations in a Box
one_liner: Turn the neighbors' informal, cash-in-a-coffee-can road fund into a recorded, insurable road association with dues, reserves and competitively bid plowing and grading.
customer: Households on private roads and shared driveways (5-60 homes per road). The urgent buyers are the real estate attorneys, title agents and listing agents whose closings stall without an enforceable road maintenance agreement.
problem: Millions of rural households reach their homes by private roads maintained by handshake. One neighbor plows, some chip in, some free-ride. Washouts and disputes are common. Lenders and title insurers often want a recorded, enforceable maintenance agreement, so sales stall. HOA software assumes an incorporated HOA with a manager, not 12 neighbors and a gravel road.
solution: Fixed-fee formation: map who benefits, draft a state-specific maintenance agreement, record it with the county, and set up a simple legal entity or association where state law allows. Then recurring service: ACH dues collection with reminders and lien-based enforcement where allowed, a reserve fund, standing bids from vetted plow, gravel and grading contractors, a photo log of road condition, and storm-damage documentation packages for county or FEMA requests.
why_now: Post-2020 in-migration put many remote workers on rural private roads. Extreme-weather washouts, such as Hurricane Helene's damage to private roads and bridges in western North Carolina in 2024, showed how many neighborhoods have no entity that can pool money or apply for repair aid. Lenders and insurers keep tightening property-access checks. No vertical software serves informal neighbor groups.
revenue_model: $1,500-3,000 formation fee, paid by the neighborhood or by the seller at closing. $12-25 per household per month for dues administration. A disclosed 5-8% procurement fee on managed contractor bids.
non_obvious_insight: The customer with urgency isn't the neighborhood but the closing. A failed sale costs a seller and an agent five figures, so attorneys and agents will send you deals for a flat fee. Recurring revenue then comes from dues float and admin. At 200 associations you are the largest single buyer of plowing and gravel in a region, which gives you procurement leverage no individual road has.
first_30_days: Pick a state dense with private roads (Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, or the North Carolina mountains). Get an attorney to draft a reusable agreement template. Partner with 3-5 real estate attorneys and title agents who see failed closings. Sell a $1,500 'closing rescue' formation package. Run 2 pilot associations with free dues collection for 6 months to prove the workflow.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: PayHOA, Mainstream HOA and community-association platforms (Buildium, AppFolio, FrontSteps, Vantaca, CINC and similar), DIY legal templates and local real estate attorneys (Nolo, US Legal Forms, LegalZoom-style forms, local attorney drafting), Public alternatives: state road-association statutes and county road or special-assessment districts. White space: Tentative. Coverage was thin, so absence of a dedicated venture-backed product is not proven. What I found unserved:
1. No product I could find bundles the closing-triggered legal package (state-specific maintenance agreement, county recording, a lightweight entity) with the ongoing administration for informal neighbor groups. PayHOA covers dues admin generically and cheaply; the statutes and the law-firm and forms market cover formation; nobody stitches them together for the 5-60 home private road.
2. Competitively bid, pooled procurement of plowing and gravel across many associations. I found no tool for it.
3. Storm-damage documentation and an organized entity ready for state or FEMA private-road aid. NC's program required a single point of contact, ownership proof and a 50% HOA cost share, so unorganized roads were poorly placed to claim.
4. The transaction-channel distribution (attorneys, title agents and listing agents at a stalled closing) looks unowned by software vendors.

Weak points:
- The recurring $12-25 per household per month is 6-12 times PayHOA's roughly $2 per household.
- Lien-based enforcement is state-dependent. NC's G.S. 136-102.6 only requires disclosure of who maintains private streets, and my Maine excerpt covered assessment authority but not liens.
- Holding dues float triggers trust-accounting and money-handling rules.
- The 5-8% procurement fee creates a conflict of interest.

title: Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers
one_liner: A neutral third party installs pre-construction sensors around proposed data centers and administers a developer-funded, automatic payout guarantee to neighbors, so permit fights run on evidence.
customer: Independent and mid-size data center developers seeking 50-500 MW campus approvals in contested counties. County commissions and state regulators are a second buyer because they can make the service a permit condition. Hyperscalers with in-house community teams are not the target.
problem: Permit fights are evidence-poor. Nobody has a pre-construction baseline of well levels, night-time noise, air quality or voltage at homes, so every later complaint about dry wells or a hum can be neither proven nor disproven. Both sides fight on feelings and lawyers. Politics has turned: New York paused environmental permits for data centers of 50 MW or more in July 2026, Texas ordered its environmental regulator to stop issuing new data center permits in September 2026, and local pauses now exist in at least 14 states. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found only 14% of Americans would welcome one nearby.
solution: Baseline-in-a-Box. Over 60-90 days before the application, deploy 30-60 low-cost sensors: property-line night noise, depth and conductivity in volunteer neighbors' wells, PM2.5, night-sky brightness, and voltage sag at homes. Publish a read-only public dashboard. Have a university extension hydrogeologist and an acoustician review the methods. Escrow the data with hash-anchored timestamps so neither side can edit it. Keep monitoring for 10 years. Then add a Neighbor Guarantee: a developer-funded escrow that pays affected households automatically, like parametric crop insurance, when verified well drawdown or noise exceedances occur. No lawsuit is needed.
why_now: In 2026 the moratorium movement jumped from town boards to governors' offices (New York's executive order of July 14, Texas's TCEQ permit halt of September 21). Developers now need social license as much as megawatts, and regulators are actively drafting the frameworks that will say what evidence counts.
revenue_model: The developer pays $75-150k per site for setup, $4-10k per month for monitoring, and an 8-10% administration fee on the guarantee escrow. Counties that write the service into permit conditions create repeat demand. Later, anonymized data licensing to regulators and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The baseline protects the developer more than the opponents. It is the only defense against future exaggerated or mistaken claims, and it turns 'trust us' into 'audit us'. Parametric payouts replace adversarial claims, which is why a rational developer buys it from a neutral party rather than opposing it.
first_30_days: Pick one county with a pending rezoning hearing (Georgia, Virginia, Indiana, Pennsylvania or Texas). Offer the developer's land agent a free 30-day pilot on 10 neighbor wells with an agricultural-extension partner. Build nodes from off-the-shelf parts at about $1.5-3k each. Present the live dashboard at the public hearing and convert that developer to a paid contract. Use the result as the case study for the next 5 developers.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: KETOS (SHIELD / KELP data-center water monitoring), Aethair (Aethair PRO, Environet, Thiamis), Envirosuite (ASX:EVS), Kunak. White space: Nobody found sells the bundle, so the status is 'gap' and not 'open'. The sensor and baseline layer is not open: KETOS (about $45M raised) pitches an independent baseline for data centers, Aethair pitches pre-construction baselines, Envirosuite has community dashboards, and consultancies bundle baselines into permitting. The unserved wedge is what sits on top of the sensors. (1) A neutral administrator holding escrowed, tamper-evident data whose governance the county and community accept, unlike developer-hired consultants and unlike opposition-side groups such as CEDS. (2) The Neighbor Guarantee: an automatic, no-litigation payout to households from a developer-funded escrow when a pre-agreed trigger is hit. No vendor, insurer, county ordinance or developer program found does this. The nearest things are Franklin County, Indiana's draft rule (escrow for 24-hour emergency potable water to impacted neighbors, plus developer-funded monitoring wells), one-off buyouts and lump-sum checks. (3) A 10-year, multi-parameter (wells, noise, PM2.5, voltage) record packaged as a permit-condition template that regulators can adopt. Weak points: the sensor baseline will commoditize; attribution is hard, because well drawdown from drought or other pumping is indistinguishable from data-center drawdown unless the design uses upgradient control wells and pumping records; automatic payouts may look like insurance under state law; and developer counsel may resist a pre-committed payout as an admission of liability. Note: the web-search budget ran out before I could check Crunchbase/YC directly for a startup doing exactly the escrow-plus-parametric bundle, so 'nobody found' means no evidence in about 25 searches, not proof of absence.

title: Independent Auditor for AI-Paid Pet Claims
one_liner: A read-only shadow adjudicator plus a cross-carrier duplicate registry that independently re-checks every auto-paid pet claim against the policy's own clauses and produces the validation records state examiners now ask for.
customer: Head of claims and the compliance officer at US pet-insurance MGAs and small carriers paying roughly 100k-400k claims a year that already auto-adjudicate through a vendor platform or in-house LLM triage. The channel is the fronting carriers whose binders give them claims-audit rights over those MGAs. Narrowest wedge: MGAs that announced automation in the last 18 months and write in the 25+ states that have adopted the NAIC AI bulletin.
problem: Once claims are auto-paid, the insurer is accountable for the model's output but cannot see inside it, and the vendor selling the automation is marking its own homework. Two failures are invisible. One is silent overpayment: excluded lines paid (exam fees, cremation, prescription diets, supplements), wrong deductible, co-insurance, annual-limit or waiting-period math. The other is wrongful denial, which means complaints and market-conduct exposure. No single carrier can see the same PDF invoice filed with two insurers, or an altered invoice that looks fine in isolation. The parent's price-based edits add a third problem: reductions land on owners as balance bills, with no vet contract behind them, so mid-size insurers will not fund them.
solution: Read-only nightly export of invoice, policy form and adjudication decision, with no workflow replacement. (1) Normalize every invoice line to a canonical code (start from VeNom, so there is no taxonomy to defend). (2) Extract each policy form's exclusions, limits and waiting periods into clause-anchored rules once per form, human-verified. (3) Re-adjudicate independently and return agree or disagree per claim with a clause citation, sorted into three queues: likely overpaid, likely wrongly denied, and duplicate or tampered (PDF metadata, font and amount forensics). (4) Produce a monthly exam-ready validation pack with sample testing, drift and complaint linkage, which is what examiners request under the bulletin. (5) Cross-carrier registry: carriers contribute only hashed fingerprints (clinic, date, total, pet identity hash, line hashes) and get match alerts. Price benchmarks appear only as informational flags. They become a reason to reduce a payment only where the policy form has reasonable-and-customary language and the carrier opts in.
why_now: NAIC's AI model bulletin has been adopted by 25 states plus DC as of July 2026, and a 12-state examiner evaluation-tool pilot runs through September 2026. Under it, insurers stay accountable for vendor model outputs, and 'we cannot see the model internals' is not accepted. Pet premiums grew about 19% in 2025 on 6.98M insured US pets, and carriers are racing to automation (Five Sigma at Odie, Lassie at about 60% automated). LLMs make clause extraction from policy forms and PDF invoice reading cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: Annual platform fee of $45k-$120k by claim volume (about $0.15-$0.30 per claim scored), including monthly exam-ready packs. Registry-only tier of $12-25k for small carriers and TPAs. Optional 15% contingency on documented overpayments prevented on contract-clear lines. Sales math, assuming a $350 average paid claim: a 200k-claim MGA pays about $70M a year in claims, so an $80k fee breaks even at about 0.11% of claim dollars. Month-12 target: 6 MGAs at $80k plus 6 registry-tier customers at $15k, roughly $570k ARR. The registry then extends to all US carriers at a per-lookup fee, an ISO-ClaimSearch-style utility for pets.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation has turned automation from a cost saver into a liability, and the vendors selling automation are structurally unable to vouch for themselves, the way an accounting firm cannot audit its own consulting work. Independence is the product, and it is a budget line that exists (compliance, delegated-authority audits) rather than one that has to be invented. Duplicate and tamper detection is the only kind of edit that gets more valuable with every carrier that joins and never requires fighting a vet or a policyholder. State anti-fraud immunity statutes generally permit sharing suspected-fraud data with anti-fraud organizations, which makes a hashed registry lawful to seed on day one.

Days 7-21: build the clause extractor on 10 public policy forms and the invoice normalizer on about 500 sample invoices. Days 14-30: cold-approach 25 heads of claims and compliance with a free 'exam-readiness shadow audit' of 2,000 of their auto-approved claims from the last 90 days. The deliverable is a one-page count of overpaid lines, likely wrongful denials and duplicates. Convert the best results to a $25k, 90-day paid pilot. Success is 3 signed pilots by day 90 and a registry seeded by those pilots' fingerprints.

title: Search-Fund Accelerator for Buying Scrap Yards
one_liner: A cohort program that turns laid-off mid-career managers into owner-operators of small scrap yards, e-scrap shops and transfer stations. It brings deal sourcing, environmental diligence and SBA-lender access.
customer: Laid-off ops, finance and product managers with severance or savings of about $100-300K, who pay cohort tuition and a success fee. Second customer: retiring owners of scrap and recycling businesses who want a successor buyer. SBA lenders are a channel.
problem: Mid-career job searches now run 7-13 months with near-zero interview rates (HN threads), and the hiring freeze is hitting degree-holders. Meanwhile thousands of owner-run recycling businesses have no successor. Their storage and processing permits take years to obtain, and domestic scrap has just become strategic: the Aug 27, 2026 BIS rule forces black mass and tungsten scrap sellers to allocate 100% of sales to US buyers. Nobody packages this asset class for a first-time buyer.
solution: Build a target database from state solid-waste and hazardous-waste permit records, scrap-dealer licenses and owner age. Provide a standard diligence pack covering environmental liabilities and Phase I/II, fire history and insurance, permit transferability, commodity exposure and offtake contracts. Add a 90-day operator bootcamp with a mentor operator and introductions to SBA lenders. Take a fixed fee at close plus a small advisory equity stake.
why_now: AI-driven hiring freezes are producing a large pool of capable managers with cash and time. Greenfield battery and plastics recycling is capital-destroying (Ascend Elements and Li-Cycle bankruptcies, 7 of about 30 US PET reclaimers closed), while boring, permitted, cash-flowing yards look safer. DoD and DOE equity stakes and the BIS allocation rule are re-rating domestic scrap.
revenue_model: Cohort tuition (about $4-6K per seat). Buy-side success fee ($25-50K or 1.5-2% at close). 2-5% advisory equity in each acquisition. Sell-side listing fees from retiring owners. Diligence-pack licensing to lenders.
non_obvious_insight: In recycling the scarce input is not technology or capital but a competent successor operator, and the labor market is now manufacturing them. Permits are the moat, so the right move is to buy permitted cash flow instead of financing new plants.
first_30_days: Pull permit and owner-age lists for two states. Run a free webinar for laid-off managers through layoff-tracker and career communities and enroll a first cohort of about 10. Get two retiring owners to sign exclusive sell-side LOIs. Sign an environmental-consulting partner for a flat-fee diligence pack, and one SBA lender as the financing partner.

title: Renewal Radar for Silent AI Exclusions
one_liner: Track carriers' filed AI exclusions and tell brokers, 90 days before renewal, which clients just lost AI coverage, then place the affirmative buy-back.
customer: Independent agencies and regional brokers (10-200 staff) with commercial books, their E&O carriers, and MGAs.
problem: Since January 2026 ISO-style generative-AI endorsements (CG 40 47 and CG 40 48) and far broader carrier forms, such as W. R. Berkley's 'absolute' AI exclusion, are attached at renewal, often buried. Clients use AI in ways they never disclosed. Brokers carry E&O exposure for failing to warn, and no tool maps which of a broker's 300 clients face AI exclusions or what AI each client actually uses.
solution: A rate and form filing scraper (public SERFF filing access) plus an endorsement parser that normalises exclusion breadth: gen-AI only versus any AI, bodily injury versus advertising injury, vendor-supplied AI. It feeds a renewal calendar imported from agency-management CSVs. A 12-question client AI-use questionnaire, optionally backed by an SSO or expense-report scan for AI tools. Output is a one-page 'AI coverage gap letter' plus a list of affirmative AI markets for placement.
why_now: 1 Jan 2027 renewals are the first big cycle after the Verisk endorsements became available, and AIG, Great American and Berkley filings landed through 2026. Affirmative AI capacity now exists (Armilla via Lloyd's, AIUC, Munich Re aiSure), so a gap and its fix can be sold together.
revenue_model: $250-800 per month per agency, $150-600 per gap letter for non-subscribers, 10-15% commission on affirmative cover placed, and $2-5k per month filing-intelligence subscriptions for MGAs and carriers.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is triggered by their own E&O fear, not curiosity about AI. The filings are public but unreadable, so the moat is a normalised exclusion database nobody at a brokerage has time to build. Silent AI cuts both ways: an unexcluded policy is a reason to ask for affirmative cover, so the gap letter also works as a sales tool for the broker.
first_30_days: Scrape SERFF filings in five large states and build the tracker. Start a free weekly 'AI exclusion tracker' newsletter aimed at 500 brokers. Offer 10 agencies a $500 concierge gap audit on their five biggest accounts. Sign one affirmative-AI MGA for placement referrals.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Patra (AI Policy Checking), Quandri, Zywave Apex / Advisor Agent, Testudo. White space: A real gap remains, but it is much narrower than the pitch. Nobody found sells a commercial-lines, broker-facing workflow that (1) takes a book's actual renewal forms schedules, quotes and binders (not just carrier-level filings), (2) detects and normalises AI exclusion breadth for each client, including bespoke wording such as Berkley PC 51380 and unnamed 'AI' language, (3) ties it to a 90-day renewal calendar, and (4) hands the producer a client-ready gap letter and a matched affirmative placement. Pieces exist separately. Patra reads commercial policies for hidden exclusions but is not AI-specific. Quandri and Zywave own the 90-day renewal trigger but show no exclusion-level AI flagging. Testudo and Armilla offer AI-use mapping and placement but only for their own paper.

Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs and ShadowLock publish free trackers, and Certian even ships CC BY 4.0 CSV and JSON. (b) A filing shows a carrier adopted a form in a state. It does not show the form is attached to client X's policy, so the real signal is the policy document, not the filing. (c) SERFF filing access covers admitted markets only. Surplus lines is where most E&O, D&O and tech-E&O AI exclusions sit, and it is largely invisible to SERFF.

Wedge that looks unserved: commercial professional-liability and tech-E&O accounts (design firms, law, accounting, software, agencies) where exclusions are broadest and most bespoke, for independent agencies without an in-house risk-advisory team, priced as a renewal-review add-on rather than a filings database.

title: Independent Post-Reform Valuation for Medical Lien Funders
one_liner: A neutral, coder-signed valuation agent that tells LOP factoring companies and the lenders behind them what their medical receivables are worth after tort reform.
customer: Regional medical-lien funders and LOP factoring companies in Florida, Texas and Georgia that buy receivables from ortho, pain, chiropractic and ASC providers, plus the warehouse lenders and private-credit funds financing them. Buyer is the funder's CFO or head of underwriting, with the lender's credit analyst as the forcing party. First target list is 30-40 funders.
problem: Funders buy receivables at a fraction of billed charges, priced on attorney reputation and past collections. Reform changes the collateral. In Florida, 768.0427 makes the LOP, coded billing, the factoring purchase price and referral relationship disclosable and admissible, and amounts actually paid become the reference point. Cases accruing after March 2023 are only now reaching settlement, so the first post-reform collection cohort is landing on funders' books. Their lenders want borrowing-base reporting and independent collateral valuation, and no neutral standard exists. Carrier vendors, plaintiff platforms and data utilities serve everyone but the person holding the risk.
solution: Phase 1, fixed-fee 'Book Audit' in 10 business days. The funder sends a de-identified export (purchase price, coded bill lines, provider NPI, attorney, venue, dates, outcomes on closed files). Output: cohort-level expected collection and time-to-cash curves under current state rules; the top-decile at-risk receivables; a signed independent valuation letter the funder can hand to its lender or investors; and a 'bid sheet' of maximum purchase price by CPT bundle, provider type, venue and attorney tier. Phase 2: per-receivable scoring at purchase and monthly re-marking through a portal or API. Phase 3: lender-appointed valuation agent, where the warehouse lender designates and co-signs the engagement and receives monthly portfolio monitoring, like a collateral field exam. The coder bench and methodology from the parent are reused, but the output is a valuation, not a courtroom opinion.
why_now: First post-reform (Florida 2023) case cohort is resolving in 2026, so books are repricing now and lenders are asking questions. Private credit has moved into esoteric legal and medical receivables, and lenders in that class expect third-party collateral valuation. Florida's mandatory disclosure of factoring purchase price means every funder now knows its own buy price is evidence against the receivable, which forces a rethink of pricing and structure. LLM bill extraction makes coding a 2,000-line portfolio in days instead of months, with coder sampling for sign-off.
revenue_model: Book Audit $15-40k per portfolio, repeated semiannually. Subscription $3-6k/month plus $12-25 per receivable scored. Lender-facing monitoring $2-4k/month per credit facility, mandated by covenant. Illustration: 30 funders at $60k/year is about $1.8M, with upside from expanding to hospital-lien, workers' comp lien and pre-settlement receivables, and eventually independent collateral valuation for rated securitizations of medical receivables, where third-party valuation is mandatory.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody has looked at LOP bills as collateral. The same benchmark that is a weapon in a deposition is a valuation input in a credit agreement, and the buyer has the best data. Funders hold the only ground-truth set of what LOP bills actually settle for, by code, provider, attorney and venue, which carriers, defense lawyers and every vendor lack. Serving funders buys that dataset and tightens every later model. The issuer-pays conflict that damaged rating agencies is solved by making the lender the appointing party and by fixed fees, like an ABL field examiner.
first_30_days: Pull UCC-1 filings (for example the Florida Secured Transaction Registry) that name medical receivables or accounts as collateral, to identify funders and the banks and credit funds financing them. Recruit two coders, one ex-ABL field examiner or credit analyst who has run a borrowing-base review, and one part-time attorney to build a rules matrix by state. Run a blind backtest pilot with 2-3 funders. They send 200-500 closed receivables with outcomes hidden, we predict the realized collection, they compare. Offer it free in exchange for permission to use the calibration. Convert the best pilot to an $18-25k Book Audit and use the result to approach that funder's lender.
