title: Immune-Graded Beef-on-Dairy Calves With Warranty
one_liner: A $1 refractometer reading at day 3-5 predicts whether a $1,400 crossbred calf lives, yet nobody independently verifies it at sale. Own that measurement and the warranty that follows.
customer: Calf raisers, backgrounders and feeder buyers who pay a premium for graded calves (or a subscription for the data), and dairies who pay to have calves graded so they can earn the premium. Later, insurers and MGAs underwriting a mortality warranty.
problem: Beef-on-dairy calf output went from about 50,000 head in 2014 to roughly 3.2M in 2024, with CattleFax projecting 5-6M, and calves have sold as high as $1,500 per head. Calf raisers buy 3-5 day old calves nearly blind and eat the 10-25% loss to scours and pneumonia. The colostrum information stays on the dairy, so raisers blame 'bad calves' and dairies blame 'bad luck'. Each dead calf now leaves a four-figure hole in a heifer pipeline that is short by hundreds of thousands of head.
solution: Independent serum total protein (Brix) testing on every calf at day 3-5, done at the dairy or at pickup by trained techs with digital refractometers and a phone app. Each calf is graded on the published four-tier passive-transfer scale (Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor) and logged with dairy, sire, weight and hydration score, then gets a QR tag or passport that follows the calf to the buyer. Buyers pay a premium for Excellent and Good and discount Poor. Phase 2 uses the accumulated data to price a 30- or 60-day mortality warranty ('we have graded 300,000 calves and know what a Brix 8.4 calf from Dairy X does'). Phase 3 gives dairies a colostrum scorecard that brokers use.
why_now: Crossbred calves are at record values, beef-on-dairy volume is doubling, and the heifer shortage means every lost calf is expensive and hard to replace. Consensus passive-transfer grading standards were published in 2020, digital refractometers are cheap, and buyers are already paying for verified genetics programs, so 'verified immunity' is the obvious next tag that nobody sells.
revenue_model: $4-6 per calf grading fee paid by the seller or split with the buyer, then $10-25 per calf warranty premium once loss data supports underwriting (partner with an insurer or MGA rather than carrying risk), plus a data subscription for larger calf raisers and feedlots.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone argues about sire genetics while the vet knows immune status dominates early death, and calves with failure of passive transfer carry about twice the risk of illness and death. The test is $1 and 60 seconds, but a number only has value when a neutral third party holds custody of it at the point of sale. The business is independent custody of the measurement, not the refractometer, and the resulting dataset becomes the underwriting moat.
first_30_days: Two vet techs, two $150 digital refractometers and a phone form. Offer free grading on 5 dairies' weekly calf shipments to 2-3 calf raisers or brokers. Ask the raiser to report 30-day illness and death by calf tag. After about 60 days, publish graded-versus-ungraded outcomes, then get one raiser to commit to a premium (for example $30-50) for Excellent calves and a discount for Poor, and charge the test fee from that point on.

Genuinely unserved: an independent, per-calf immunity record that travels from dairy to raiser to feeder to packer, plus a neutral dispute-resolution measurement.

title: Payoff-Triggered Refund Recovery for Credit Unions
one_liner: A payoff-desk plug-in that finds the unearned GAP and service-contract refunds the moment a member pays off, and applies unearned add-on credits in repossession deficiencies. It goes through lenders, not SEO, so it reaches the borrowers the consumer refund sites can't.
customer: Credit unions and regional auto lenders (payoff and collections departments). The lender pays a small SaaS fee or takes a share of recovered money. Second wedge: consumer bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid, at $99 per deficiency audit.
problem: When a borrower pays off early, trades in, or has the car totaled or repossessed, they are owed the unearned pro-rata part of GAP, service contracts and other financed add-ons. Refunds are not automatic. Not the dealer, not the lender and not the administrator processes them, and consumer-refund sites exist because so few people claim. The incentives point the wrong way. The dealer suffers a commission chargeback, so it stalls. The administrator profits from non-cancellation. The lender never owned the product. The borrower doesn't know. In repossession, unearned add-on credits should reduce the deficiency the borrower is sued for, and they rarely appear on deficiency notices. Roughly 3M repossessions a year and subprime 60+ day delinquency at a 32-year record of 6.9% in January 2026 make this a very large pool of missed money.
solution: Ingest the closed-loan document image or loan tape, read the itemized products and financed amounts from the retail installment contract, and match each to its administrator. Compute the pro-rata or earned-basis refund by state rule (New Jersey, for example, requires an automatic refund within 60 days). Auto-generate the cancellation packet with the lender's payoff letter, odometer statement, signature or letter of authority, and the state statute citation, then track it to payment. Stalled cases escalate to the state insurance department with a complaint file. The moat is a database of roughly 60 administrators' actual cancellation requirements and response behavior, plus the 50-state rule set. The repossession product reconciles deficiency notices against the same data and outputs an attorney-ready exhibit.
why_now: Record delinquencies and about 3M repossessions a year, roughly 84-month loans with about 30% of trade-ins underwater, and long terms mean most loans die early and carry stacked add-ons. Credit unions are under member-experience and fee-optics pressure, and California's SB 766 now requires dealers to keep refund and cancellation records. LLMs can finally read messy contract images and cancellation forms cheaply enough to run at scale.
revenue_model: Credit union pays $3 to $6 per payoff processed, or 20 to 30% of recovered money with no upfront fee. Attorneys pay $99 per deficiency audit or a $499 per month subscription. Later, sell aggregated administrator refund-speed benchmarks to dealer groups and regulators.
non_obvious_insight: The consumer refund sites that exist all have the same weakness: they wait for the borrower to show up. The one moment every party knows the loan ended is the payoff, and the lender's payoff desk is the only place that sees all of them. The refund itself comes from the administrator's pool, and the dealer's chargeback is a fight between the dealer and the administrator. The borrower's claim doesn't depend on the dealer cooperating, so the dealer stalling does not need to hold up the refund.
first_30_days: Build the administrator playbook for the 20 largest GAP and service-contract administrators and the 10 highest-population states. Offer 3 credit unions a free retrospective audit of 500 payoffs from the last 12 months and show them the dollar total of unclaimed refunds. Take a 30% success fee on live recoveries. Simultaneously give 5 consumer bankruptcy attorneys the repossession deficiency audit free on their next 3 cases in return for case studies.

2. Genuinely unserved and specific, if the market read holds:

   - A 50-state pro-rata rules engine combined with an administrator-by-administrator cancellation-requirements database.

That helps demand, as a compliance and UDAAP driver, but it changes the pitch from 'find hidden money' to 'reduce liability'.
   - A 20-30% success fee taken from a member's own refund has poor fee optics for a credit union. It also conflicts with the idea's own member-experience rationale.
   - On payoff, the refund goes to the borrower, so the CU gets no direct economic benefit. The CU's incentive is goodwill and compliance, not revenue.
   - CU vendor due diligence and core/LOS integration will make the sales cycle slow.
   - The California SB 766 citation in the idea did not check out. The leginfo summary I fetched for the 2023-24 bill described an unrelated social-worker licensing bill. Do not rely on that cite until it is confirmed.

title: Refund-Netted Dating: Wholesalers Fund the Float
one_liner: Sell regional wholesalers and buying groups a claim-underwritten '28-day MFP dating' program that defers payment on MFP-drug invoice lines and nets them against the refund, so the pharmacy never borrows and the wholesaler is paid a dilution-risk fee to us.
customer: The independent-pharmacy channel head or CFO at regional full-line wholesalers, independent buying groups and non-wholesaler-owned PSAOs. These are the first wave because they can decide in weeks and cannot out-finance the Big 3 on other terms. The franchise programs of the Big 3 (Good Neighbor Pharmacy, Health Mart, Leader) come second. The pharmacy is the beneficiary, not the payer of record.
problem: The wholesaler owns the weekly auto-debit, the invoice detail and, as a possible third-party support entity, a view into refund flows. It is the cheapest and best-placed capital in the system. But the float squeezes its customers. NCPA-cited behavior includes 70% of pharmacies limiting stock of high-cost drugs and 60% using personal or business savings. That means lost brand volume, rising credit exposure to weakened accounts, and closures (SCPC warns 60% of its members may close). Wholesalers have not extended MFP dating at scale because they see invoices, not claims. They cannot tell which MFP refunds are safe or price the dilution risk of reversals, disputes and 340B rejections. Outside lenders sit behind the wholesaler's debit and cannot fix this.
solution: 'MFP Dating Desk' is software plus a capped dilution guarantee. 1) Connect the wholesaler's invoice and EDI feed with each participating pharmacy's PMS claims export and MTF remittance files, with the pharmacy's consent given inside the wholesaler's normal account flow. 2) Each week, match MFP-drug invoice lines to eligible claims and score dilution risk. 3) The wholesaler moves those lines into a 28-day bucket, or nets them against the refund where it already handles payment routing. 4) We cover dilution losses above the pharmacy's holdback, up to a cap, funded by our reserve and excess capacity from a credit fund or licensed carrier. The guarantee is structured as contractual recourse or through a licensed carrier so it is not unlicensed insurance. 5) The pharmacy sees one dashboard showing what is deferred and when the refund clears. Extended trade terms are commercial credit, not a loan, which avoids most of the lending-license and disclosure work in offspring one.
why_now: In January 2026 the refund lag became a recurring weekly mismatch between 14-day wholesaler terms and a 21-day refund average. On January 1, 2027 semaglutide and 14 other drugs join and the mismatch grows. Independents are choosing wholesalers and buying groups for 2027 terms, so a cash-flow feature is a retention weapon. CMS now expects manufacturers to include cash-flow mitigation in their refund plans, which shows the problem is recognized but unsolved on the distribution side.
revenue_model: The wholesaler pays a platform fee of about $5k a month plus about $10 per active pharmacy, and a risk-and-data fee of about 0.25-0.5% of the deferred refund amount per cycle, calibrated to measured dilution. The wholesaler recovers this through a small service fee. The pharmacy's all-in cost lands near 8-12% annualized, in line with bank A/R lines and well below an MCA. Illustrative: a regional wholesaler with 300 senior-heavy accounts averaging $50k of float has $15M deferred at any time. That is roughly $0.4-0.9M a year of risk fee before losses. Add more wholesalers and buying groups without adding a lending license.
non_obvious_insight: The parent treated the wholesaler as an obstacle. It is actually the best-collateralized lender in the chain, because it holds the debit right, the invoice line item and the relationship. It does not lack capital. It lacks a price for statutory-refund dilution, and that price lives in claim-level data it does not own. Selling underwriting to the party that owns the rails turns a capital-intensive 15-25% lending business into a small fee on a much larger base. It also removes the CAC problem, because the wholesaler's sales reps are the distribution.
first_30_days: List 15 regional wholesalers, buying groups and independent PSAOs and reach the CFO or independent-channel head through association conventions and cold outreach. The pitch is a free 'MFP exposure map' built from their own invoices. Aim for one 60-day shadow pilot with no cash at risk, covering 20-30 senior-heavy accounts. Compare what the deferral would have cost against measured dilution, and use it to set the fee. In parallel, get indicative excess-of-loss terms from one credit fund or specialty carrier and check with counsel whether the guarantee needs a license.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SpendMend (MFP Rebate Reconciliation), Plenful (MFP Intelligence / MFP Command Center), ScriptPro Financial Advantage, Liberty Software (and other PMS vendors, e.g. PioneerRx, PrimeRx, Redsail). White space: Verdict: gap, and a narrow one. In roughly 27 searches across varied terms (MFP refund advance, bridge loan, factoring, fintech, PSAO program, wholesaler program) I found NO product that specifically underwrites and advances against MTF-remitted MFP refunds. Pharmacy lenders sell generic A/R and MCA lines, and the MFP players only sell reconciliation. The unserved space is a claim-level underwriting and servicing capability for refund dilution risk: 340B lesser-of rejections (RARC N907 inappropriate rejections), reversals, Good Faith Inquiry disputes, and authorized-generic refund amounts. It is most valuable for borrowers whose float is large: LTC/senior-care pharmacies, 5-50 store groups, and possibly 340B covered entities in the HRSA rebate pilot, where the float is $8.9M-$208M a year for hospitals (Health Affairs). It also applies to the January 2027 step-up when semaglutide joins.

The wedge is weak in five ways.
1. The 'free missing-refund report' is already crowded: SpendMend, Plenful ($76M raised), ScriptPro, Liberty, and free Beacon MFP dashboards.
2. A typical independent's float is small, about $11k a week or $27k a month per NCPA. At 15-25% APR that is roughly $4-7k a year of gross revenue per pharmacy, before losses and a cost of funds of 8-10%. Customer acquisition through state associations and Facebook groups will be costly relative to that.
3. Wholesalers control the payment path. Cardinal routes MFP refunds through Central Pay and wholesalers auto-debit weekly, so a lender's sweep sits behind the wholesaler in practice. Cardinal customers cannot easily direct refunds to a lender-controlled account.
4. 'Non-recourse' is hard to deliver. Manufacturers can reverse refunds and CMS's own materials describe reversals when claims prove ineligible, so a lender will need pharmacy recourse or holdbacks. That undermines the 'prime paper' insight.
5. Policy is a moving target. CMS made manufacturers include cash-flow mitigation plans in their MFP effectuation plans (accelerated refunds, self-identification). NCPA is still pushing CMS and manufacturers for faster payment, including in Sept 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance.

Adjacent generic lenders can also just add MFP refunds to a borrowing base.

Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and open-source sweeps were not fully run. 'No direct competitor found' means not found, not proven absent. | How this version avoids them: Reconciliation vendors (SpendMend, Plenful, ScriptPro, Liberty, Beacon) sell to the pharmacy or health system and end at a report. We sell to the wholesaler and end at a credit decision, so we are not in their category. The Big 3 are listed as adjacent competitors that own the rails. Here they are the eventual channel, not a rival. They can build it but are slow, and the regionals cannot build it at all. No pharmacy borrows, so there is no 15-25% versus 8-12% pricing fight with Live Oak, Corporate Capital Direct, ARF or other lenders, and no borrowing-base conflict with the pharmacy's bank. Wholesaler payment priority is the design, not a risk. The main risk is a Big 3 in-house build. The defenses are speed in the regional segment and a licensable neutral data layer.

title: Tooling Title Diligence for Small-Brand Acquirers
one_liner: A fixed-fee, 5-day report that tells buyers of $2M-$50M product companies which molds the target legally owns, where they physically sit, and whether the factory is already selling the target's product.
customer: Buyers of physical-product brands and small manufacturers with China-made tooling: search-fund and ETA searchers, independent sponsors, lower-mid-market PE platforms and SBA 7(a) acquirers. The channel is business brokers (Quiet Light, Empire Flippers, FE International-type firms), M&A attorneys and SBA acquisition lenders. The payer is the buyer, at the LOI-to-close stage. Secondary payer is the seller, who pays for a pre-listing 'tooling-ready' file.
problem: In a small-brand acquisition the molds are the asset that everyone values at zero. The QoE accountant sees an expensed PO line, the lawyer sees a boilerplate 'all assets used in the business' rep, and the seller often cannot say whose name the tools are in or whether a bill of sale exists. If the factory holds the tools, the buyer has bought a business that the supplier can hold hostage for a 30% price hike, and the buyer also cannot move production, which matters more now that tariff rules keep changing. Nobody in the deal owns this question: brand-protection vendors sell to the brand, not to the buyer, and audit firms do not cover tooling.
solution: 'Tooling Title and Leakage Report', delivered in 5 business days. (1) Tool schedule: every tool, its location, its condition, and who holds title (bill of sale, PO language, tool-ownership clauses, supplier confirmation letters). (2) Leakage test, which is the parent's $2,500 overrun audit repurposed: buy 10 units from 1688, Alibaba, Temu and Amazon third-party sellers, and compare them with the golden sample and lot codes to say whether the supplier is already selling the product. (3) Portability score: what it would cost and how long it would take to move each tool or re-cut it, with quotes from a US or Mexican molder. (4) Deal remedies: draft closing conditions, a tool bill-of-sale assignment, custody and release agreements, and a holdback or escrow sizing suggestion for the buyer's lawyer to use. The on-site audit is optional and subcontracted, passed through at cost, and only for deals over $10M.
why_now: The searcher and ETA wave and retiring owners are pushing more small manufacturers and brands to market. The Amazon aggregator unwinding put many product brands up for resale with tooling and supplier problems. Tariff volatility (the Feb 2026 IEEPA ruling per the parent research) makes 'can this brand switch factories?' a live diligence question, where in 2019 it was rarely asked. Remote marketplace scanning has become cheap enough to fit inside a fixed fee.
revenue_model: $4,900 per report, paid by the buyer, usually as a closing cost. Seller pre-listing file $2,500 through brokers. Post-close '100-day tool sovereignty plan' $12k (title cure, fingerprint baseline, second-source quotes). Portfolio monitoring for PE sponsors $2,000/month per physical-product company. Model: 240 reports a year at month 12 is about $1.2M, plus a 25% attach rate on the plan (60 plans at $12k) is about $0.7M. Reachable market is assumed at roughly 1,500 physical-product deals a year, to be validated with brokers. Lenders or brokers might pay for reports on deals that later close.
non_obvious_insight: This is the same asset as the parent idea, but a far better moment to sell it. A breakup victim only hires you once they are already hurt and have already lost leverage. An acquirer is at peak willingness to pay, because they are about to wire $5M, and the report's cost is rounding error on the deal. The finding also turns straight into money: a missing bill of sale becomes a closing condition, a holdback or a price cut. A short-lived supplier concentration risk becomes a negotiating chip. Diligence is also the top of a repeat-customer funnel, since a sponsor with 6 platform companies buys monitoring on all of them.
first_30_days: Build a redacted sample report from public listings and a mock data room. Pitch 6 brokers and 3 searcher communities, offering 3 free reports on live deals, in exchange for testimonials and a written referral agreement, since a diligence step that reduces buyer fear helps brokers close deals. Then sell 5 paid reports at an introductory $3,500. Get one M&A attorney to endorse the closing-condition language. Line up two China audit contractors by referral for the on-site option. Kill signal: brokers refuse to introduce the report to buyers, or no buyer will pay $3.5k.
lineage: mutation of I0552 ('Supplier Divorce Protection: Tool Census and Overrun Forensics'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Harris Sliwoski (China Law Blog), Alitheon (FeaturePrint), Red Points, Corsearch (Zeal 2.0, Investigations 360, Distribution Control). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch quota (200 per session) was already used up when I started, so I could not run the planned 6-12 searches. I also could not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or open-source repos. The findings below come from about 25 direct page fetches, so treat 'nobody does this' as unproven. The vendors most likely missed are the many small China-based QC and sourcing agents that sell 'mold audits' and 'mold relocation', plus PI and investigation firms (Kroll-type). Do a manual pass on those before committing.

What I found: I found no productized, US-facing service that bundles (a) a serialized tool census, (b) cavity-level physical fingerprints, and (c) marketplace test-buy attribution of overruns to a specific tool. The problem is documented and treated as an unproductized legal-advice problem: Harris Sliwoski tells clients to keep an inventory form and audit quarterly, and never mentions a third-party vendor for it. Marketplace monitoring and takedown (Red Points, Corsearch, Alibaba's free IP platform) is commoditized and crowded. Object fingerprinting exists (Alitheon) but is aimed at electronics, aerospace and gray-market diversion, not tool-mark attribution.

Genuinely unserved: (1) cavity-level 'which tool made this part' attribution that holds up as evidence; (2) a tooling census standard for mid-market OEMs, timed to the exit window; (3) an evidence pack designed for counsel that a brand-protection vendor's screenshot-and-takedown workflow does not produce.

Weak points: Extraction (tool 3) is freight, customs and re-qualification work that sourcing agents and forwarders already do at low margin. Monitoring (tool 2, first half) is a commodity. Attribution is legally useful only when the overrun carries the client's IP (trademark, design patent, trade dress) and the client can enforce it. If the part is generic or unbranded, a match proves little. Chinese-court enforceability is unproven here. | How this version avoids them: Red Points and Corsearch sell takedown subscriptions to brands and have no deal-time product for a buyer or a lender. QIMA runs supplier audits without tooling-title verification, and is too slow and costly for a $3M deal, so it becomes a subcontractor for large deals. Harris Sliwoski sells legal hours after a dispute, so we are the fact base their M&A-side peers lack. Alitheon and MoldTrax do not play in deal timelines. Sourcify is a natural post-close channel for the re-sourcing step. Accounting-based QoE and general legal diligence firms are the real adjacent substitutes, and they do not physically verify tools or test the marketplace (assumption, to check in the 20 first conversations).

title: Yen Gap Audit for Legacy Seven Owners
one_liner: A flat-fee LINE audit that takes HQ's own AI order proposal as the baseline and shows Kansai multi-store Seven-Eleven owners, per item and delivery slot, the yen gap between what HQ suggests and what their own 15/85 contract says they should order.
customer: Owner-operators (individuals or small corporations) running 3 to 10 legacy-contract Seven-Eleven stores in Osaka, Kyoto and Hyogo, who have a contract renewal or a new-store offer within 24 months. Legacy stores are the narrow wedge because Seven's new contract (50/50 disposal share, effective autumn 2027) applies only to newly opened stores with no conversion planned, so the 15/85 asymmetry persists on existing stores for years. Multi-store owners are the segment that can pay (a 5-store owner pays about 34k yen a month against roughly 4.7M yen of food discarded per store per year), that is most exposed to OFC pressure, and that faces the legacy-versus-new-contract expansion decision. One chain means one contract model. Lawson and FamilyMart wait until their subsidy formulas are verified.
problem: HQ's AI proposes a quantity but never says whose payoff it maximizes. With an 85% owner share of disposal loss, the owner's critical ratio is about 22% (keeps about 24 yen per rice ball sold, loses about 85 yen per one binned) while HQ's is about 70% (earns about 36, loses about 15). Owners cannot audit the proposal and fear the OFC if they deviate. Judges flagged three weaknesses: the asymmetry fades on post-2027 contracts, HQ's markdown push since May 2024 (about 300 items, alerts about 2 hours before expiry) commoditizes a markdown clock, and willingness to pay for software is unproven. Earlier framing as a competing ordering AI also invites a fight with three chains' in-house AI.
solution: Not a better forecaster, a payoff transform. If HQ's recommended quantity approximates the 70th percentile of demand and the owner's optimum is the 22nd, the owner's cut is about 1.3 standard deviations of the slot's demand spread (about 3.9 units for an item averaging 10 with a spread of 3). The tool therefore needs only the HQ proposal (photo of the order terminal screen or printout), the order actually placed, and the store's hourly sales history to estimate the spread. It returns (1) a ranked Yen Gap sheet: the ten biggest expected-yen differences per delivery slot between HQ's proposal and the owner-optimal quantity under that store's own royalty tier and disposal share; (2) an audit of HQ's markdown clock: for the roughly 300 alerted items and for non-alerted items, whether 'two hours before expiry' is earlier or later than the owner-optimal sticker time given the store's sell-through curve; (3) a neutral 'why I ordered differently' one-pager citing expected value under the owner's contract, shown to the OFC only if the owner chooses; (4) a monthly portfolio page with each store's critical ratio and true hourly wage after royalty and own labor, plus an annual memo on whether the next store should be a legacy expansion or a new-contract store. Nothing touches HQ systems.
why_now: Osaka's minimum wage rises 54 yen to 1,231 yen on 1 Oct 2026 and Diamond reported a Seven internal simulation with franchisee profit falling to about one third if wages rise on flat sales. HQ AI ordering is now default at all three chains, so owners follow suggestions they cannot audit. Seven's June 2026 announcement of a new contract with a 50% disposal share concedes the point, and creates a two-tier portfolio (legacy versus new stores) that owners have never had to model. Photo OCR of Japanese printouts and cheap LLM-based structuring make a per-owner concierge audit affordable in 2026, which was not true in 2019.
revenue_model: Entry offer: a paid 30,000 yen '30-day Yen Gap Audit' on one store (credited toward the first 3 months), which tests willingness to pay before any subscription. Then a flat 6,800 yen per store per month (bundle discount at 5+ stores). An annual 150,000 yen next-store-or-renewal decision memo, timed to the moment an owner holds a real 10M-yen decision. Optional 15% gain-share only where a signed baseline exists, so revenue does not depend on disputed savings. Ex-OFC consultants and accountants who refer owners get a 20% revenue share. Bottom-up, if about 5,000 legacy stores sit with 3+ store owners in this segment (an assumption to verify), that is roughly 400M yen a year at full penetration.
non_obvious_insight: The forecast is not the scarce thing, the payoff is. HQ's proposal already encodes a demand distribution, so an owner-side tool can back out the implied quantile and shift it, needing only a spread estimate from the owner's own sales sheets. That makes the product tiny to build and easy to back-test on the founder's three stores. It also flips the political framing: the owner is not overriding HQ's AI, he is applying his own contract to its numbers. Counter-positioning is real, since HQ cannot ship a screen that says its AI is tuned to the wrong payoff without conceding the conflict the JFTC and METI panel already scrutinize.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: back-test on the founder's three stores, comparing HQ proposals against realized sales and disposals, estimating the implied quantile and spread per category, and computing the yen gap. Day 3: one-hour paid review by a franchise lawyer of the confidentiality and third-party data clauses. Days 8-20: sell 10 paid 30,000-yen audits through 3-5 ex-OFC consultants, one or two accountants serving multi-store owners, and Kansai owner LINE and Facebook groups. Kill or pivot signal: fewer than 3 paid at 30,000 yen. Days 21-30: deliver audits, convert the willing to 6,800 yen flat with a 60-day money-back guarantee, and publish a one-page legacy-versus-new-contract critical-ratio table (22% versus about 36%) as owner-to-owner content.
lineage: mutation of I0272 ('Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Seven-Eleven Japan AI ordering plus HQ-led markdown (Eco da Ne), Lawson AI.CO (ordering plus AI markdown recommendation), FamilyMart AI Recommend Ordering, Sinops (sinops-CLOUD AI markdown) with Sato. White space: No product found that is an independent owner-side payoff engine for Japanese convenience-store franchisees. Searches in Japanese and English returned no startup, SaaS or app that (a) uses the owner's actual royalty tier and disposal-share contract terms to compute order levels, (b) sets markdown timing from the owner's payoff, or (c) audits HQ AI recommendations against the owner's interest. HQ tools (Seven, Lawson, FamilyMart) cover order and markdown outputs but are HQ-controlled and aimed at waste or sales, not owner take-home. Supermarket AI-markdown vendors (Sinops/Sato, Wasteless) sell to retailers, not franchisees. The union and ex-OFC consultants give advice with no calculators or automation. Caveats: (1) Seven-Eleven's new contract (announced June 2026, effective autumn 2027) raises HQ's disposal-loss share from 15% to 50% (with a cap), lowers charge to 53%/67%, applies only to newly opened stores with no conversion planned for existing stores (https://www.ryutsuu.biz/strategy/s061915.html, https://www.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/news/2118977.html). At 50/50 the owner critical ratio rises from about 22% to roughly 36%, so the asymmetry mostly fades on new-contract stores but persists on legacy stores for years. (2) Seven's HQ-led markdown push since 2024 partly commoditizes the markdown clock. (3) The 22% vs 70% math checks out for the 85/15 split, but contract terms differ by chain (Lawson subsidy formula is more complex, FamilyMart is about 15%), so each chain needs its own model. The product does not compete on forecast accuracy and audits HQ's markdown clock instead of inventing another. Sinops/Sato and Wasteless/Afresh/Shelf Engine sell to retailers and inherit the retailer's payoff, and none uses a franchisee's contract terms. Too Good To Go is an outlet for surplus, not a decision tool. The Okayama union and ex-OFC consultants give advice without calculators, so they become referral partners rather than substitutes, and the channel does not depend on the small Okayama union. Narrowing to legacy Seven stores avoids the per-chain contract complexity and the shrinking-asymmetry problem of post-2027 new stores.

title: Continuity Retainer for One-Licensee Funeral Homes
one_liner: Key-person insurance for funeral homes: a bench of pre-credentialed licensed directors and embalmers who step in within 24-48 hours when the owner is sick, burned out or gone, with a built-in path to succession.
customer: Independent and rural funeral homes with one or two licensed staff (roughly 30-150 calls a year), typically owner-operators aged 55-75. A second buyer is the family of an owner who has died or fallen ill and needs the home kept legal while it is sold.
problem: States require a licensed funeral director or manager-in-charge, and often a licensed embalmer, for an establishment to operate. The owner is on call 24/7/365 and hasn't had a real week off in years. One heart attack, surgery or burnout means the home cannot legally operate, families get funneled to the consolidator down the road, and a business built over three generations is sold at a distressed price. Informal 'relief director' phone lists exist, but there is no bench, no contract, no reciprocity or board paperwork handled, and no guarantee anyone answers at 3 a.m.
solution: Recruit retired and semi-retired licensed directors and embalmers, including many leaving consolidators, and pre-credential them in a target state cluster with background checks and reciprocity filings. Sell continuity retainers that guarantee a set number of coverage days a year (real vacations, weekends off) plus emergency activation within 24-48 hours at a day rate. The company handles the state-board notice of interim manager changes. A succession track lets an interim operator or next-generation licensed buyer convert into a partner or buyer with seller financing, so owners have an alternative to a roll-up.
why_now: Consolidation keeps shrinking the independent pool (SCI alone bought about 22 funeral homes and 2 cemeteries for roughly $101M in 2025). The licensed workforce is aging while mortuary-school pipelines are thin. Rising cremation lowers revenue per case, making full-time second hires unaffordable for small homes. Rural closures are creating 'funeral deserts'. Many states have passed occupational-license recognition laws that make multi-state relief staffing easier.
revenue_model: Retainer of $900-$2,000/month per home including N coverage days. Activation day rate of $800-$1,400 billed to the home, with a 25-30% margin over what the licensee is paid. Per-case fees for trade embalming and prep-room services. A 1-2% success fee on succession transactions.
non_obvious_insight: The real asset of an independent funeral home isn't the building, it's one license holder with a phone, and that is a single point of failure. Consolidators know it and wait. Owners will pay to sleep: this is a wellness and continuity product disguised as staffing, and its best feature is the succession pipeline it creates once a trusted operator is already inside the home.
first_30_days: Recruit eight retired licensed directors and embalmers through state association chapters and retiree groups. Check each state board's rules for temporary manager-in-charge designation. Pitch 20 one-licensee homes in two adjacent counties at a $1,200/month founding rate with a 'test weekend off' guarantee. Sign the first three, and run the first covered weekend within 30 days to produce a testimonial.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: NFDA Funeral Career Hub and NFDA recruiting services, NFDA succession planning member resources and SESCO HR consulting, Selected Independent Funeral Homes (staff recruitment and Selected Transfer Services), American Mortuary Service (trade embalming and removals, Dallas/Fort Worth). White space: Caveat first: this verdict has low-to-moderate confidence. The WebSearch budget for the session was already exhausted (200 of 200), so none of the planned 6-12 searches ran. I did not use WebFetch on a search engine to get around the limit. All I did was fetch about 15 specific vendor and industry URLs. Most guessed domains did not resolve, and the ones that resolved were adjacent players, not direct competitors. "No direct competitor found" therefore means "not found with a very limited method", not "verified absent".

What the limited evidence supports as unserved: (1) A contracted, pre-credentialed, multi-state bench with a guaranteed activation SLA. The only related products I could confirm are a job board (NFDA), an association recruiting and transfer program (Selected), trade embalming vendors (American Mortuary Service) and member-only succession content (NFDA). None of them takes on the license-holder single point of failure. (2) The bundled path from interim operator to succession buyer with seller financing. I found nobody offering it, and it is the strongest differentiator because it turns a cost centre into a deal pipeline.

Risks I could not verify and that could still kill or reshape the idea, all of which come from the idea file and general reasoning, not from research:

If temporary designation is unavailable in the target states, the 24-48 hour activation promise fails legally. Check this first, state by state.

- Liability, insurance and non-solicit exposure when a stranger runs someone else's establishment.
- Supply. A bench of eight retirees has to be dense enough to reach homes in rural counties within 24 hours, so density in one cluster matters more than breadth.

title: Widow-First Retention Drills for Wealth Advisors
one_liner: Sell independent advisors an annual 'if one of us dies' rehearsal for couples, because the defection risk sits at the first spouse's death, not with the kids.
customer: Independent RIAs and small wealth teams ($150M-$2B AUM) whose median client is 65+. The buyer is the firm principal or COO.
problem: The industry spends on next-gen events with heirs. Cerulli says about $54T of the transfer is spousal and about $40T of that goes to widowed women. The survivor is grieving, holds a house full of logins and unknown accounts, and has to decide whether to keep the advisor. Advisors are commonly said to lose most widows within a year (widely cited, verify). The cause is usually friction, not performance.
solution: A 90-minute 'Survivor Fire Drill' run by the advisor's team with a software kit. Each spouse's death is simulated in turn. The tool builds a First-90-Days playbook: who to call, which accounts exist, which autopays must keep running, and where the documents are. It audits titling and beneficiaries from the survivor's point of view and flags single points of failure, such as only one spouse knowing the passwords. It then schedules pre-agreed advisor check-ins at day 3, 14, 45 and 90. The advisor gets a dashboard of which couples have done the drill and where their exposure is.
why_now: Cerulli's Sept 2026 work frames retention of the transfer as the priority, and 89% of surveyed firms call family meetings essential. Wealth managers are buying heir-engagement tools, yet the first wave of money is spousal and the widow is under-served. Cheap document ingestion and secure vaults make the kit affordable for small firms.
revenue_model: $300-$700 per household per year billed to the firm, or a $25-40K/yr platform fee for a 100-household book. The ROI pitch: keeping one $1.5M widow at a 1% fee is worth $15K a year.
non_obvious_insight: The heir-retention narrative aims at the wrong person on the wrong day. Widows rarely leave over portfolio returns. They leave because nobody made the first 90 days easy. A rehearsal also works where estate planning fails, because people avoid 'planning' but will attend a scheduled drill.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-5 RIAs through advisor communities and podcasts. Run drills by hand with a spreadsheet and printed binder for each firm's 10 oldest couples. Record time-to-locate-accounts and the number of single-point-of-failure findings. Charge a $2.5K pilot fee and turn the findings into a retention case study the advisor can show prospects.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Empathy (LifeVault + Loss Support), Everplans (Enterprise / advisor channel), Trustworthy (Family Operating System), Wealth.com. White space: Nobody found sells the specific wedge: a facilitated, scheduled couples rehearsal of the first spouse's death, run by the advisor's team. The software layer is commoditized (Trustworthy at $10 per client per year), so the defensible white space is the ritual, the audit method and the outreach cadence, not the vault.

title: Load Recovery for Municipal Utilities and Co-ops
one_liner: Sell the verified dead-plant record to the municipal electric utilities and rural co-ops that lose money every month the anchor plant sits dark, priced as a package plus a bonus tied to the load they get back.
customer: Municipal electric systems, rural electric co-ops and their joint-action agencies or statewide associations (for example American Municipal Power and the state municipal electric associations) in OH, PA, MI and IN, where an anchor industrial plant has closed and the utility's own economic-development or general manager decides. Wedge: 8 utilities in the Mahoning Valley, Akron/Canton and western PA with an idle plant of at least 2 MW in their territory.
problem: When a plant with several MW of load closes, a small public utility keeps paying its fixed wholesale power, transmission and substation costs but spreads them over fewer kWh, so rates rise for homes and shops and the remaining industrial customers get nervous (an assumption to validate with 10 utility managers). These utilities have no economic-development staff, are ignored by the investor-owned-utility databases and grid-analytics vendors, and cannot tell a data-center or battery developer what is actually inside the fence of their dead plant. Meanwhile the plant's energized service, which the utility itself installed and meters, is the one asset that could replace the lost load.
solution: A 'Load Recovery Package' per idle plant: (1) electrician-verified one-line diagram, gear nameplates, spare capacity and slab/crane condition; (2) the utility's own historical interval load and substation loading, which only the utility holds, turned into a stranded-load scorecard showing what re-energizing 2, 4 or 8 MW would do to fixed-cost recovery and rates; (3) a pre-cleared economic-development rate rider and a written will-serve position, drafted with the utility's engineer, which is the hardest input in the parent's product and is free when the utility is the customer; (4) outreach to a curated buyer list (manufacturers, battery and cold-storage operators, small data-center and inference developers) with the record as the data room. Later, a member-services version sold through a joint-action agency to all members.
why_now: Buyers with real money now want existing energized industrial shells, so a dead plant in a small utility's territory has more than one class of possible buyer for the first time in decades. Large-load tariffs and interconnection queues at the big investor-owned utilities push developers to look for capacity elsewhere, and roughly 128-week transformer lead times make existing service worth years. Ohio's 125+ local data-center moratoriums are a problem for pure data-center strategies, so a buyer-agnostic pitch to friendly municipal utilities is safer.
revenue_model: $9,500 per Load Recovery Package paid from the utility's economic-development budget; $18,000 per year retainer covering up to five sites, buyer outreach and a rolling record refresh; a capped performance bonus of about 10% of the first-year demand-charge margin from re-energized load (cap around $60k), structured as an economic-development services fee from the utility and not a commission on a property sale (have Ohio counsel confirm the real-estate licence question before signing). Channel: a joint-action agency or state association licenses the tool to members at $40k-$80k per year. Bottom-up: about 100-150 qualifying utilities in four states at an average $12k in year one is $1.2M-$1.8M, with 70-plus percent gross margin after the electrician cost on the package.
non_obvious_insight: The utility, not the broker or the manufacturer, is the party that already holds the two hardest inputs, years of interval meter data on the dead plant and the ability to say in writing what it would take to re-energize it, and it is also the only party that loses money every month the plant stays dark. Sell to them and the will-serve letter that costs the parent weeks of chasing becomes something the customer hands you. Small public utilities are also unserved by every funded competitor, which all chase hyperscalers and the big investor-owned utilities.
first_30_days: Week 1: build a list of every municipal electric system and co-op in northeast Ohio and western PA (from state association member lists) and match each to idle plants using Ohio EPA and county parcel data; shortlist 20 with a dark plant of at least 2 MW. Weeks 2-3: call 20 general managers and superintendents; pitch a free 'stranded-load scorecard' on their dead plant using their meter data. Get three to share interval data and access. Week 4: deliver one scorecard plus a paid quote of $9,500 for the full package, and pitch a 20-minute slot at a state municipal electric association meeting. Success test: one utility signs the $9,500 package or a letter of intent, and one association agrees to a member pilot.

White space: Nobody I found productises a building-level, physically verified 'inside-the-fence' record for dead Midwest plants. That record would cover the electrician-verified main service size, voltage, gear age and nameplates, spare capacity, slab and crane-rail condition, the state of the existing air and wastewater permits, and a utility will-serve letter, all in a scored, comparable format sold before the deal. The funded players (LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces) work at the substation and grid level and are aimed at data centers. Utility and state databases (JobsOhio, AEP, FirstEnergy, ZoomProspector) verify sites and utility service, not building gear or permit status. Scout and Brownfield.ai are the closest competitors, but they look desktop- and network-led with no per-building inspection, and I found no evidence they carry electrician-verified data. The genuine gap is a trusted, standardised, seller-commissioned building electrical and permit record, not the parcel-scoring layer, which is already crowded and funded. The idea's weaker points: the Ohio permit-transferability wedge is thin (see evidence), and it is unproven that brokers will pay $1.5k-$3.5k. | How this version avoids them: GridCARE, LandGate, Enverus and Paces work at substation and grid level for data-center developers and large investor-owned utilities, and none inspect inside the fence. AEP, FirstEnergy, JobsOhio and ZoomProspector are free or embedded databases of sites and buildings that do not verify gear and are irrelevant to small public utilities without such programs. Scout and Brownfield.ai are network and listing platforms for buyers and owners with no utility-side product and no meter data. The customer here has no productised alternative, only the general manager's phone calls, and the utility's own data is a cornered resource the funded competitors cannot get at a small utility unless they are invited in.

title: Verified AI Coverage Levels for Vendor Contracts
one_liner: Invert the parent by checking the vendor's insurance from the counterparty's side. AI-enabled vendors upload their policies and get an independent, shareable 'AI Coverage Level' (L0-L3) with monitoring, so enterprise procurement teams can write 'L2 or higher' into contracts. Over time that makes it the insurance-sufficiency standard for AI vendors.
customer: Payer: AI-enabled software and services vendors of 10-300 staff (SaaS with AI features, dev and marketing agencies, MSPs, fintech and health-tech vendors) who sell to banks, health systems and other regulated enterprises with insurance clauses in their MSAs. Free users: enterprise general counsel, TPRM and procurement teams. Later payers: those enterprises' portfolio-monitoring subscriptions, and vendor-compliance and trust-center platforms embedding the check by API.
problem: Enterprise MSAs require vendors to carry, for example, $5M tech E&O and $5M cyber. Proof is a certificate of insurance, which shows limits, carrier and expiry but not exclusions. An absolute AI exclusion in the E&O policy makes the certificate hollow for exactly the failures the buyer worries about (a hallucinated output that costs money, model-vendor data leakage, generated-content IP claims, an autonomous action). The vendor rarely knows, because the broker did not flag the endorsement. The buyer relies on coverage nobody has read, and the indemnity is only as good as the vendor's balance sheet. The insured is the party least motivated to find out its coverage is hollow, so it never gets found. (I could not run web checks in this session to confirm that no COI tracker already reads endorsement wording, so treat that as an assumption to verify first.)
solution: First product, sellable within 6 months: the 'AI Coverage Attestation'. The vendor or its broker uploads the policies and endorsements, and the same diff and classification engine runs. An independent reviewer signs a one-page output. It shows the level and, for four AI failure modes (erroneous output, IP infringement from generated content, data leakage through a model provider, autonomous action), whether each is covered, excluded or silent, plus retro date and whether defence costs sit inside limits. The vendor gets a shareable live link for procurement teams and trust centers. Monitoring re-verifies at every renewal or cancellation and alerts the vendor and anyone who holds the link. The published levels run from L0 (absolute or any-AI exclusion), L1 (gen-AI exclusion with carve-backs), L2 (silent, with no AI exclusion) to L3 (affirmative AI cover). The buyer gets a free portal and an 'AI insurance rider' clause library, so a GC can write 'vendor must hold L2 or higher' into an MSA. Vendors at L0 or L1 are given a neutral list of affirmative markets, but nothing in the model depends on placement.
why_now: Enterprise AI procurement is now standard, and AI addenda in MSAs and security questionnaires are spreading. Vendors renewing on 1 Jan 2027 will be the first large cohort to lose AI coverage silently, just as customers' contracts assume it. Trades Coverage counted 2,369 AI exclusions in force by 31 July 2026, so the exposure exists at scale. Trust-center tools have made 'share evidence by link' the normal way to close security reviews, and AIUC-1 shows that buyers accept an AI assurance standard when it is credible. Long-context extraction over policy PDFs is what makes independent attestation affordable.
revenue_model: Vendor pays $900-2,400 per year per attestation including monitoring, or $250 for a rush one-off when a deal is waiting. Enterprise portfolio monitoring for 200+ vendors is $12-30k per year. Platform API checks are $20-60 each. Affirmative-market referral fees are a later, secondary line. These are estimates to test. The payer is the vendor, because a tick-box that blocks a six-figure deal is worth far more than the fee.
non_obvious_insight: This flips the buyer chain. The party that relies on the coverage, and holds contractual leverage, is the one who can force a hundred vendors to verify, so the value of the credential rises with each buyer that references it. That is a network effect broker software does not have. It also sidesteps the duty-to-advise weakness, because the obligation is contractual, not tort-based. And the level scheme lets an independent attestor become the standard, while carriers cannot credibly grade their own wording and the AI-liability carriers have a conflict.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: interview 20 vendor CFOs and founders and 10 GC or TPRM leads, and collect 5 real security questionnaires or MSAs that contain an AI-insurance question. Days 8-20: run 10 free attestations on real policies from vendors who agree, and publish Levels v0.1 with one redline rider clause. Days 15-30: pre-sell 5 attestations at $500 to vendors with a live deal blocked on the question, and pitch 2 trust-center or COI platforms for a pilot integration. Kill signal: if fewer than 3 of the 20 buyers can name a deal or contract review where the insurance question mattered, the counterparty pull is not there.
lineage: mutation of I1133 ('Renewal Radar for Silent AI Exclusions'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Patra (AI Policy Checking), Quandri, Zywave Apex / Advisor Agent, Testudo. White space: A real gap remains, but it is much narrower than the pitch. Nobody found sells a commercial-lines, broker-facing workflow that (1) takes a book's actual renewal forms schedules, quotes and binders (not just carrier-level filings), (2) detects and normalises AI exclusion breadth for each client, including bespoke wording such as Berkley PC 51380 and unnamed 'AI' language, (3) ties it to a 90-day renewal calendar, and (4) hands the producer a client-ready gap letter and a matched affirmative placement. Pieces exist separately. Patra reads commercial policies for hidden exclusions but is not AI-specific. Quandri and Zywave own the 90-day renewal trigger but show no exclusion-level AI flagging. Testudo and Armilla offer AI-use mapping and placement but only for their own paper.

Three parts of the plan are weak. (a) The SERFF scraper and exclusion database are not a moat. Trades Coverage already compiled 4,078 records for free. Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs and ShadowLock publish free trackers, and Certian even ships CC BY 4.0 CSV and JSON. (b) A filing shows a carrier adopted a form in a state. It does not show the form is attached to client X's policy, so the real signal is the policy document, not the filing. (c) SERFF filing access covers admitted markets only. Surplus lines is where most E&O, D&O and tech-E&O AI exclusions sit, and it is largely invisible to SERFF.

Wedge that looks unserved: commercial professional-liability and tech-E&O accounts (design firms, law, accounting, software, agencies) where exclusions are broadest and most bespoke, for independent agencies without an in-house risk-advisory team, priced as a renewal-review add-on rather than a filings database. | How this version avoids them: Testudo, Armilla, AIUC, Mount and Munich Re/Mosaic sell AI cover, so their grading of the market is conflicted. This is an independent attestor that routes to them. AIUC-1 is the nearest standard, but it certifies AI-agent controls and is tied to AIUC's own insurance, whereas this rates whether a vendor's existing insurance responds. Patra, Quandri, Zywave, Rosella and FurtherAI check policies for brokers or carriers, so their buyer is different and their output is a workflow, not a credential a counterparty can rely on. The free trackers (Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs, ShadowLock, Trades Coverage) are carrier-level and cannot verify a particular vendor's policy. Adjacent and unverified in this session: COI trackers and trust-center vendors, which I expect to check limits and expiry and not endorsement wording, so a partnership route is likely, and one to check first.

title: Flight simulator drills for county SNAP eligibility workers
one_liner: Short daily drills using synthetic cases built from the state's own error taxonomy, sold to county social-services directors who are about to pay for every eligibility mistake.
customer: County social services / DSS directors and supervisors in county-administered SNAP states (NY, NC, CA, OH, MN, CO, VA) and the state associations of counties. Buyers pay $12k-25k per county per year, or $150-300 per worker. States can buy statewide at $150k-500k.
problem: H.R.1 raises the state/county share of SNAP administrative costs from 50% to 75% starting October 2026. From October 2027, states with payment error rates of 6% or higher must pay part of benefit costs. In New York, St. Lawrence County faces an extra $776,000 in year one, Jefferson County over $1 million and Warren County $415,000. The state's error rate is 13% against a 6% line, a penalty of about $1B statewide, described as 'a missile heading right at New York State'. North Carolina's error rate is 6.69%, with state cost-share exposure of about $140M at 5% and $420M at 15%. The state's advice to counties is 'documenting, documenting, documenting'.
solution: A 15-minute daily micro-drill for eligibility workers: a synthetic household case (pay stubs, shelter costs, household composition changes, address changes) with a realistic case-file packet, where the worker computes eligibility and benefit. The drill feeds back the exact error that federal QC would cite. Cases are generated from the state's policy manual and the public USDA QC error categories (wage reporting, household size, address changes and shelter deductions are the common ones), with no real client data. Supervisors see per-worker error-type heatmaps and a coaching queue. Later: an optional second-look review desk staffed by former QC reviewers that samples a county's real closed cases.
why_now: The error-rate look-back, cost-shift start (October 2026) and penalty tiers (October 2027) create a hard two-year clock. Louisiana is paying cash bonuses to error spotters, Kansas hired an outside consultant, Virginia is buying technology for error checking, and NC is running monthly QC webinars and targeting high-error counties. States are visibly buying error-reduction help, and there is no standard product for it.
revenue_model: Per-worker annual subscription ($150-300) or flat per-county fee ($12k-25k); statewide contracts through the state SNAP office or county association; add-on per-case second-look review at $18-30/case.
non_obvious_insight: A county with a 0% error rate is still penalized if the state averages above 6%, so no county can solve this alone and the real buyer is the state or the association pooling county money. Meanwhile individual county directors are hurting now and have discretionary admin budgets and training budgets they can spend without an RFP. Synthetic cases avoid the PII and system-access barrier that blocks most govtech vendors in benefits programs, so a small team can start selling in weeks, not after a FedRAMP-style review. Evidence: county exposure and 13% New York error rate (https://www.northcountrypublicradio.org/news/story/53929/20260910/snap-cost-shift-pushes-north-country-counties-into-a-financial-bind); NC official on documentation, targeted training and CQI (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9949745/north-carolina/executive/organizations/state-departments-and-agencies/mental-health/developmental-disabilities-and-substance-abuse-services/state-official-urges-counties-to-cut-snap-payment-error-rate-to-avoid-hr1-cost-shares); state remediation tactics such as bonuses, outside consultants and new training (https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/states-scramble-cut-snap-error-214614305.html).
first_30_days: Build 40 synthetic cases across the top error elements from one state's manual, with a scoring engine. Approach the state county association's SNAP resource group and 5 county DSS directors with a free 30-day pilot with a pre/post test on 10 new hires. Publish a 'your error rate in dollars' calculator for county commissioners. Convert the two most engaged counties to paid annual plans priced below their discretionary-purchase limits.

Competitor check: GAP. White space: Caveat on confidence: my WebSearch budget ran out before I could run any searches, so this is a partial check. It rests on direct fetches of about 15 URLs (the idea's cited sources, Maximus, PCG, PSI, Code for America, Kognito, Relias, Deloitte, Route Fifty) plus GitHub repo searches. Several sites returned 403, 404 or 503. It could not cover Crunchbase, Product Hunt, YC or TechCrunch, or find startup names. What looks unserved: (1) No product I found gives eligibility workers a daily, scored, synthetic-case drill tied to the specific federal QC error elements (wages, household composition, shelter and address changes) with per-worker error-type heatmaps. Maximus's Accuracy Assistant explicitly works 'side-by-side' in live cases and does not train. Code for America and PolicyEngine are systems and rules tools. Kognito-style simulation vendors never targeted eligibility work. The main threats are structural rather than competitive: (a) the real buyer is the state, which typically owns training (state academies, mandated curricula, training environments in the state eligibility system), and county discretionary budgets may not cover $12k-25k; (b) Maximus or a state's existing LMS vendor could add a practice module; (c) policy variation across states (BBCE, standard utility allowance, county practices) makes per-state case libraries costly to build and keep current; (d) an open-source rules engine (PolicyEngine) lowers the barrier for copycats.

title: Community Lenders Pool Orders to Keep County Appraisers
one_liner: Sell rural credit unions and banks a pooled, multi-year county 'appraisal continuity compact', where their combined order flow plus a fixed capacity retainer makes a retiring appraiser's territory viable for a supervised successor.
customer: Payer: the 4-8 community banks and credit unions that originate mortgages in a rural county cluster whose appraiser is retiring, each paying about $3-8k a year, bought through state credit union leagues, bankers associations and their service arms or CUSOs. Beneficiaries: the retiring appraiser (paid a fixed stipend), a mid-career certified appraiser from an adjacent county acting as supervisor, and 1-2 career-changer trainees (agents, inspectors, adjusters).
problem: A rural lender places 30-100 appraisal orders a year. No single small lender can sustain a trainee, and none is big enough to make an out-of-county appraiser drive 60 miles. When the county's only appraiser retires, orders go to distant AMC panel members, closings slip and purchase loans are lost. Trainee programs like Valligent's assume one lender commits volume. The retiree's book was stable because 15 direct lenders each sent about a dozen orders, so each lender was individually too small to replace it.
solution: 'County Compact': (1) Diagnose at-risk counties by joining board rosters (active certified appraisers and license age) with HMDA originations by lender and county. (2) Sign a 3-year compact among 4-8 lenders in the county: pooled first-look on local orders (lenders still order directly and independently, with no link to value conclusions or loan approval), a turnaround SLA such as 7 business days, and a fixed annual capacity retainer paid to us. (3) Recruit and equip the continuity team: a certified supervisor plus 1-2 trainees, with desk QC and UAD 3.6 tooling. (4) Pay the retiree a fixed 12-month knowledge-transfer stipend for the recorded local-knowledge interview, adjustment grids, neighborhood boundary notes and lender introductions. The retiree does not sign reports and gets no percentage of anything. (5) Give each lender a quarterly turnaround and quality report for their compliance and board files. Money flow: borrower pays the appraisal fee through the lender at the customary fee, 100% to the appraiser firm with no skim or split. Lenders pay us the retainer. We pay the retiree a fixed stipend and the supervisor a per-trainee capacity stipend. Counsel to confirm the retainer is independent of order outcomes and that we stay under state AMC registration thresholds (roughly 15 appraisers per state, to verify) because lenders order directly.
why_now: UAD 3.6 goes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 and veterans are choosing to quit. ABA Banking Journal and CSBS have documented rural appraiser shortages in 2026. The AQB exposure draft that drops the college-degree requirement widens the trainee pool. EO 14393 signals regulators want more appraiser supply. State leagues and bankers associations already sell shared services to small members, so the channel exists.
revenue_model: Capacity retainer of $3-8k per lender per year scaled by originations, so about $30k a year for a 6-lender compact, on 3-year terms. Add-on lender-paid collateral QC or desk review at roughly $45 per report. 10% distribution share to the league or CUSO. Rough economics (assumptions): year 1 costs are about $10k retiree stipend, $10k supervisor and trainee capacity stipends and $5k ops and QC, leaving a thin margin. Years 2-3 drop the retiree stipend, giving about 45-50% gross margin at steady state. 50 compacts is about $1.5M a year.
non_obvious_insight: Small lenders are each below the minimum viable volume for any successor, but pooled they equal the retiree's book. The compact re-creates that pool contractually. Lenders are not paying for appraisals, which borrowers still cover, but for the option value of local capacity, priced like a rural fire district. A single delayed or lost purchase loan costs a lender more than its share of the retainer, so 2-3 saved closings a year pay for it. Paying supervisors a capacity stipend funded by the pooled retainer solves supervisor scarcity without taking a cut of trainee fees, so fee-splitting rules are avoided.
first_30_days: Build a county risk map for TX, OH, PA and CO from board rosters and HMDA and NCUA/FFIEC lender lists, and shortlist 15 counties with an aging appraiser and 4+ community lenders. Call appraisal or ordering managers at 20 credit unions and banks and ask which orders were delayed or unplaceable in the last 12 months and what each cost. Offer two state leagues or bankers associations free county risk maps for their members as the door-opener and ask for a pilot. Recruit 2 supervisors and 4 trainees. Get a signed letter of intent for 2 pilot compacts of 3+ lenders each. Commission one counsel memo on appraisal independence and AMC thresholds.
lineage: mutation of I1039 ('Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: LIA Administrators (Appraisal Institute-endorsed E&O program), OREP (Appraisal Insurance), a la mode TOTAL / Cotality (also ACI, ClickFORMS), Aloft Appraisal. White space: No company found that bundles the four pieces (workfile custody plus subpoena and board-inquiry response, tail, local-knowledge capture, direct-lender client handoff to a supervised successor). Searches for retiring-appraiser succession services, workfile custodian services, and appraiser practice brokers returned only DIY articles from WorkingRE, McKissock, Appraisal Today and NAR.

Specific white space that survives:
(1) Third-party workfile custody and retrieval (agent-of-record for subpoenas and board requests) for retired or deceased appraisers. USPAP requires retention and retrievability for 5+ years, with regulators able to act later, and no dedicated vendor was found. Software vendors and cloud storage only store files, and nobody answers a subpoena for you.
(2) Local, rural or community-lender-funded succession. Aloft, Valligent and Solidifi are national or AMC-centric, not local continuity for a single county.
(3) The retiree-as-mentor stipend and earn-out structure, which none of the trainee programs use.

Specific weaknesses in the idea:
(a) The 'tail is frightening and costly' pain is largely solved for long-tenured appraisers by free LIA and OREP retirement tails. The paid pain is limited to those with short E&O tenure, gaps, or sub-5-year policies. Tail brokerage commissions are therefore thin.
(b) Fee-splitting and finder's-fee rules. Minnesota (82B.20) bans commission-splitting, rebates and finder's fees with appraisers, and other states have similar rules. An earn-out on inherited client revenue and a 20-30% take on trainee fees may be illegal in some states unless structured as a sale of a business or as employment.
(c) Supervisor-of-record is not passive. State rules limit trainee counts (Aloft cites 3 per supervisor), require certification in good standing and the supervisor's own E&O, and make the supervisor take full responsibility. A retiree who stays on as supervisor is not really retired and keeps license, CE and E&O costs.
(d) Client transferability is weak. Appraisal Today notes practices under $200K are 'buying a job', and residential lender relationships are 'fickle'. Most practices sell at 0.33-0.5x revenue with seller financing, and AMC-dependent revenue is not transferable.
(e) Pipeline substitutes are growing: PAREA, AXIS/CRN trainee-inspection reform, Valligent and Aloft paying supervisors. | How this version avoids them: Valligent is national, hires supervisors as employees and relies on a single lender's volume commitment, with no retiree knowledge handoff. This is a county-pooled, multi-lender contract with fixed stipends and no employment. Aloft is a centralized company-appraiser model, not local continuity. Solidifi and AXIS are AMC mentor-matching programs, while this is lender-funded capacity in named counties. PAREA gives experience without supervisors but transfers no local knowledge and does not guarantee anyone orders. Reggora and the AMC consolidators (Class Valuation, Atlas VMS) are platforms and cannot easily offer a multi-lender contractual pool for one county. LIA, OREP and a la mode do not touch this. Fixed stipends and no percentage of trainee or successor revenue avoid the fee-splitting and earn-out legality problems, and the retiree does not need to stay licensed.
